BASIC STRUCTURE AND FUNCTION OF BONE
The adult human skeleton is composed of 206 bones accounting for
<12% of body weight. Bone functions include mechanical support,
force transmission, internal organ protection, and mineral homeostasis,
and it also serves as the major site of hematopoiesis during postnatal
life. Bone consists of extracellular matrix and several cell types.
Matrix
The extracellular component of bone, the matrix, is composed of osteoid
(35%) and minerals (65%). The latter, primarily hydroxyapatite
[Ca (PO ) (OH) ], gives bone its hardness and serves as a repository for

produced by osteoblasts and contributes to the regulation of bone
formation, mineralization, and calcium homeostasis; it may also have
additional metabolic effects. Serum osteocalcin levels are used as a
specific marker of osteoblast activity. Bone maturation and metabolism
are also sensitive to cytokines and growth factors and are thus
regulated by diverse inputs, which include locally and systemically
produced factors, as well as mechanical force.
Bone matrix can be woven or lamellar ( Fig. 26.1 ). Woven bone is
produced rapidly (e.g., during fetal development or fracture repair), but
the haphazard arrangement of collagen fibers imparts less structural integrity
than the parallel collagen fibers of lamellar bone. Woven bone is
always abnormal in adults, but its presence is not specific for any particular
disease. Long bones are composed of a dense outer cortex and a

Most bones that form during embryogenesis develop from a cartilage

cartilage matrix mineralizes during apoptosis and is invaded by capillar-

synthesis. Most calcified cartilage matrix is ultimately resorbed, leaving

nous ossification, in which a dense layer of mesenchyme is directly os-

deposition of new osteoid on a preexisting surface, a process called
appositional growth.

Remodeling occurs within the bone (or basic) multicellular unit (BMU), which consists of a locally coupled “unit” of osteoblast and osteoclast activity on the bone surface. Osteoclast attachment, bone resorption, osteoblast attachment and proliferation, and, finally, matrix synthesis occur sequentially within the BMU.

Events within the BMU are regulated by cell-to-cell interactions, cytokines, and several signaling pathways (Fig. 26.4). One pathway involves three factors: (1) the transmembrane receptor activator for NF-κB  (RANK),  which  is  expressed  on  osteoclast  precursors;  (2) RANK ligand (RANKL), which is expressed on osteoblasts and marrow stromal cells; and (3) osteoprotegerin (OPG), a secreted decoy receptor made by osteoblasts and several other types of cells that binds RANKL and thus prevents its interaction with RANK. When stimulated by RANKL, RANK signaling activates NF-κB, which is essential for the generation and survival of osteoclasts. A second important pathway involves macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF), a factor produced by osteoblasts that is also crucial for the generation of osteoclasts. Finally, Wnt proteins produced by osteoprogenitor cells bind to LRP5 and LRP6 on osteoblasts to activate β-catenin signaling and OPG synthesis (Fig. 26.5). Conversely, osteocytes produce sclerostin, which inhibits Wnt/β-catenin signaling, thereby reducing bone formation. The importance of these pathways is emphasized by rare germline mutations in the genes encoding OPG, RANK, RANKL, LRP5, and sclerostin, all of which severely disrupt bone metabolism and produce congenital bone disorders (described later).

The balance between bone formation and resorption is modulated by RANK and Wnt signaling. For example, because RANKL and OPG oppose one another, bone resorption or formation can be favored by increasing or decreasing the RANK-to-OPG ratio. DEVELOPMENTAL DISORDERS OF BONE
AND CARTILAGE
Developmental abnormalities of the skeleton result from germline
mutations and become apparent during the earliest stages of bone
formation. By contrast, acquired diseases usually appear in adulthood.
The spectrum of disorders of bone development is broad, and there is
no standard approach to their classification; we will categorize the
major diseases according to their pathogenesis.
Developmental anomalies can result from localized disordered
migration and condensation of mesenchyme (dysostosis) or global
disorganization of bone and/or cartilage (dysplasia). Dysostoses may
occur in isolation or as part of more complex syndromes and are caused
by defects in mesenchymal condensation and differentiation into cartilage anlage. The most common forms include complete absence of a
bone or entire digit (aplasia), extra bones or digits (supernumerary
digit), and abnormal fusion of bones (syndactyly, craniosynostosis).
Genetic alterations that affect genes encoding transcription factors (especially homeobox genes), cytokines, and cytokine receptors are especially common among dysostoses. In contrast, dysplasias arise from
mutations in genes that control development or remodeling of the entire skeleton. In bone biology, the term dysplasia is used to imply abnormal growth and does not denote a premalignant lesion (Chapter 7).
More than 350 skeletal dysostoses and dysplasias are recognized,
most of which are extremely rare. The classification has evolved from
clinical and radiographic descriptions to one centered on the causative
genetic defects. Table 26.1 lists some of the better characterized developmental abnormalities and their associated defective genes. The relationships between specific mutations and phenotypes are complex;
different point mutations in a single gene (e.g., COL2A1) can produce
distinct phenotypes, while mutations in disparate genes (e.g., LRP5,
RANKL) can lead to similar phenotypes.
Defects in Nuclear Proteins and Transcription Factors
Defects in transcription factors, especially homeobox proteins, result
in disorganized mesenchymal condensation and dysregulated osteoblast and chondrocyte differentiation, leading to abnormal bone development.

• Loss-of-function mutations in RUNX2 result in cleidocranial dysplasia, an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by patent
fontanelles, delayed closure of cranial sutures, Wormian bones
(extra bones that occur within a cranial suture), delayed eruption of
secondary teeth, primitive clavicles, and short stature.

1068 CHAPTER 26 Bones, Joints, and Soft Tissue Tumors
Defects in Hormones and Signal Transduction Proteins
Achondroplasia is the most common skeletal dysplasia and a major
cause of disproportionate short stature. It is an autosomal dominant
disorder caused by gain-of-function mutations in the fibroblast growth
factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) gene, ,90% of which stem from new mutations in the paternal allele. Upon binding to its cognate ligand, FGF,
FGFR3 activation normally inhibits endochondral growth. This effect
is exaggerated by FGFR3 gain-of-function mutations. The delayed
cartilage growth results in shortened proximal extremities, an enlarged
head with bulging forehead (frontal bossing), and depression of the
root of the nose. These skeletal abnormalities are not usually associated
with changes in longevity, intelligence, or fertility.
Thanatophoric dysplasia, the most common lethal form of dwarfism, is characterized by diminished proliferation of chon drocytes
and disorganization of the zone of proliferation Like achondroplasia,
thanatophoric dysplasia is caused by gain-of-function mutations in
FGFR3, but the mutations in thanatophoric dysplasia r esult in stronger
FGFR3 signaling activity and thus a more severe phenotype. It occurs
in approximately 1 in 20,000 live births. Affected individuals have
disproportionately short (micromelic) limbs, frontal bossing, relative
macrocephaly, a small chest cavity, and a bell-shaped abdomen. The
underdeveloped thoracic cavity leads to respiratory insufficiency, and
these individuals frequently die at birth or soon after.
Defects in Extracellular Structural Proteins
Mutations in the major bone and cartilage collagens (types I, II, IX, X,
and XI) give rise to highly variable disorders ranging from lethal disease to premature osteoarthritis (OA).
Type I Collagen Diseases (Osteogenesis Imperfecta)
Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI), or brittle bone disease, is the most
common inherited disorder of connective tissue. Approximately
80% to 90% of OI cases are caused by autosomal dominant mutations
in the genes encoding the a1 or a2 chains of type I collagen that
result in impaired type I collagen synthesis. OI principally affects
TABLE 26.2 Subtypes of Osteogenesis Imperfecta
bone, but other tissues rich in type I collagen (joints, eyes, ears, skin, and
teeth) are also impacted. Normal collagen synthesis and extracellular
transport require triple helix formation. Many of the over 800 causative
collagen mutations identified in patients with OI result in the replacement of a glycine residue within the triple-helical domain with another
amino acid, leading to misfolding of collagen polypeptides and defective
assembly of higher-order collagen chains. Mutant collagens also interfere
with assembly of wild-type collagen chains, exerting a dominant negative
effect that explains the autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. A minority (10% to 20%) of OI is caused by mutations in other genes that variously
control collagen synthesis, osteoblast signaling, or m ineralization.
The fundamental abnormality in OI is too little bone, resulting in
extreme skeletal fragility. Other findings include so-called blue sclerae,
caused by decreased collagen content that makes the sclera translucent,
allowing partial visualization of the underlying choroid; hearing loss
related to a sensorineural deficit and impeded conduction due to abnormalities in the bones of the middle and inner ear; and dental imperfections (small, misshapen, and blue-yellow teeth), secondary to dentin
deficiency.
For treatment and prognosis, most cases of OI are clinically categorized into four major subtypes of varying severity (Table 26.2). Mutations that result in decreased synthesis of qualitatively normal collagen
are associated with mild skeletal abnormalities. Individuals with type I
OI have a normal life span but experience childhood fractures that
decrease in frequency following puberty. More severe or lethal phenotypes are associated with mutant collagens that interfere with triple
helix formation. Type II OI, which is uniformly fatal in utero or during
the perinatal period, is characterized by extraordinary bone fragility
and multiple intrauterine fractures (Fig. 26.6).

1068 CHAPTER ₂₆ Bones, Joints, and Soft Tissue Tumors
Defects in Hormones and Signal Transduction Proteins
Achondroplasia is the most common skeletal dysplasia and a major
cause of disproportionate short stature. It is an autosomal dominant
disorder caused by gain-of-function mutations in the fibroblast growth
factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) gene, ,90% of which stem from new muta-
tions in the paternal allele. Upon binding to its cognate ligand, FGF,
FGFR3 activation normally inhibits endochondral growth. This effect
is exaggerated by FGFR3 gain-of-function mutations. The delayed
cartilage growth results in shortened proximal extremities, an enlarged
head with bulging forehead (frontal bossing), and depression of the
root of the nose. These skeletal abnormalities are not usually associated
with changes in longevity, intelligence, or fertility.
Thanatophoric dysplasia, the most common lethal form of dwarf-
ism, is characterized by diminished proliferation of chon drocytes
and disorganization of the zone of proliferation Like achondroplasia,
thanatophoric dysplasia is caused by gain-of-function mutations in
FGFR3, but the mutations in thanatophoric dysplasia r esult in stronger
FGFR3 signaling activity and thus a more severe phenotype. It occurs
in approximately 1 in 20,000 live births. Affected individuals have
disproportionately short (micromelic) limbs, frontal bossing, relative
macrocephaly, a small chest cavity, and a bell-shaped abdomen. The
underdeveloped thoracic cavity leads to respiratory insufficiency, and
these individuals frequently die at birth or soon after.
Defects in Extracellular Structural Proteins
Mutations in the major bone and cartilage collagens (types I, II, IX, X,
and XI) give rise to highly variable disorders ranging from lethal dis-
ease to premature osteoarthritis (OA).
Type I Collagen Diseases (Osteogenesis Imperfecta)
Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI), or brittle bone disease, is the most
common inherited disorder of connective tissue. Approximately
80% to 90% of OI cases are caused by autosomal dominant mutations
in the genes encoding the a1 or a2 chains of type I collagen that
result in impaired type I collagen synthesis. OI principally affects
TABLE 26.2 Subtypes of Osteogenesis Imperfecta
bone, but other tissues rich in type I collagen (joints, eyes, ears, skin, and
teeth) are also impacted. Normal collagen synthesis and extracellular
transport require triple helix formation. Many of the over 800 causative
collagen mutations identified in patients with OI result in the replace-
ment of a glycine residue within the triple-helical domain with another
amino acid, leading to misfolding of collagen polypeptides and defective
assembly of higher-order collagen chains. Mutant collagens also interfere
with assembly of wild-type collagen chains, exerting a dominant negative
effect that explains the autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. A minor-
ity (10% to 20%) of OI is caused by mutations in other genes that variously
control collagen synthesis, osteoblast signaling, or m ineralization.
The fundamental abnormality in OI is too little bone, resulting in
extreme skeletal fragility. Other findings include so-called blue sclerae,
caused by decreased collagen content that makes the sclera translucent,
allowing partial visualization of the underlying choroid; hearing loss
related to a sensorineural deficit and impeded conduction due to abnor-
malities in the bones of the middle and inner ear; and dental imperfec-
tions (small, misshapen, and blue-yellow teeth), secondary to dentin
deficiency.
For treatment and prognosis, most cases of OI are clinically catego-
rized into four major subtypes of varying severity (Table 26.2). Muta-
tions that result in decreased synthesis of qualitatively normal collagen
are associated with mild skeletal abnormalities. Individuals with type I
OI have a normal life span but experience childhood fractures that
decrease in frequency following puberty. More severe or lethal pheno-
types are associated with mutant collagens that interfere with triple
helix formation. Type II OI, which is uniformly fatal in utero or during
the perinatal period, is characterized by extraordinary bone fragility
and multiple intrauterine fractures (Fig. 26.6).

and Transporters)

Pathogenesis
Most of the mutations underlying osteopetrosis interfere with acidification
of the osteoclast resorption pit, which is required for the
resorption of calcium hydroxyapatite within the matrix by osteoclasts.
For example, a mild autosomal dominant form of osteopetrosis
is caused by mutation of CLCN7, which encodes a proton-chloride
exchanger on the osteoclast cell membrane that is required for
resorption pit acidification. Similarly, most cases of autosomal recessive
osteopetrosis are caused by a mutation of TCIRG1, which encodes
1

necessary for acidification of the resorption pit. Other causes of
autosomal recessive osteopetrosis include defects in carbonic anhy -
drase 2 (CA2), which like other carbonic anhydrase isozymes generates
protons and bicarbonate from carbon dioxide and water. CA2 facilitates
both resorption pit acidification by osteoclasts and urinary
acidification by renal tubular epithelial cells. Osteopetrosis due to CA2
mutations is, therefore, accompanied by renal tubular acidosis. Alternatively,
mutations in the X-linked gene IKBKG, which encodes

inhibitor of kappa B kinase (IKK) complex, causes osteopetrosis by
impairing NF-κB function, osteoclastogenesis, and osteoclast survival
(see Fig. 26.4 ).

and hydrocephaly are often seen, resulting in postpartum mortality.
Affected individuals who survive into their infancy have cranial nerve
defects (optic atrophy, deafness, and facial paralysis) and repeated—
often fatal—infections because of leukopenia due to reduced marrow
space and decreased hematopoiesis. Compensatory extramedullary
hematopoiesis may lead to hepatosplenomegaly. Autosomal dominant
forms are milder and may not be detected until adolescence or adulthood when discovered on x-ray studies, either incidentally or because
of repeated fractures.
Osteopetrosis was the first genetic bone disease treated with
hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, which is effective because
osteoclasts are derived from hematopoietic precursors. The normal
osteoclasts produced from donor stem cells reverse many of the
skeletal abnormalities.
Diseases Associated With Defects in Degradation of
Macromolecules
Mucopolysaccharidoses
The mucopolysaccharidoses, discussed in Chapter 5, are lysosomal
storage diseases. They are caused by deficiencies in enzymes, primarily acid hydrolases that degrade dermatan sulfate, heparan sulfate, and keratan sulfate. Mesenchymal cells, such as chondrocytes,
degrade extracellular matrix mucopolysaccharides. In these diseases, mucopolysaccharides accumulate within chondrocytes and
induce apoptosis. Extracellular mucopolysaccharide accumulation
leads to structural defects in articular cartilage. Consequently,
many of the skeletal manifestations of the mucopolysaccharidoses
result from abnormalities in the cartilage anlage, growth plates,
costal cartilages, and articular surfaces. Affected individuals are
frequently of short stature and have chest wall abnormalities and
malformed bones.
KEY CONCEPTS
Developmental Disorders of Bone and Cartilage
Abnormalities in a single bone or a localized group of bones are called dysostoses and arise from defects in mesenchyme migration and condensation. They
manifest as absent, supernumerary, or abnormally fused bones. Global disorganization of bone and/or cartilage is termed dysplasia. Developmental abnormalities can be categorized by the associated genetic defect.
• Transcription factors: Homeobox genes, such as HOXD13, are frequently
mutated in brachydactyly syndromes.
• Signal transduction molecules: FGFR3 mutations are responsible for achondroplasia and thanatophoric dysplasia, both of which manifest as dwarfism.
• Structural proteins: Mutations in the genes for type I collagen underlie most
types of osteogenesis imperfecta, characterized by defective bone formation and skeletal fragility (brittle bone disease).
• Metabolic enzymes and transporters: Mutations that interfere with
osteoclast acidification of the resorption pit or osteoclastogenesis cause
osteopetrosis, in which bones are hard but brittle (marble bone disease).
Depending on the gene mutated, extraskeletal manifestations may also be
present.
METABOLIC DISEASES OF BONE
Osteopenia and Osteoporosis
Osteopenia refers to decreased bone mass; osteoporosis is defined
as osteopenia that is severe enough to significantly increase the risk
of fracture. Radiographically, osteoporosis is considered bone mass at
least 2.5 standard deviations below mean peak bone mass in young
adults, whereas osteopenia is 1 to 2.5 standard deviations below the
mean. The disorder may be localized to a certain bone or region, as in
disuse osteoporosis of a limb, or may involve the entire skeleton. Most
generalized osteoporosis is primary but a minority of cases result
from endocrine, gastrointestinal, or other underlying conditions or
from drugs (Table 26.3). Each year, nearly 2 million Americans experience an osteoporosis-related fractures, which are associated with
with an estimated cost of $57 billion.
Pathogenesis
Although numerous factors affect bone mass, the most common
forms of osteoporosis are senile and postmenopausal. Peak bone
mass is achieved during young adulthood. Its magnitude is influenced
by hereditary factors, especially polymorphisms in the genes that affect
bone metabolism (Fig. 26.8). Physical activity, muscle strength, diet,
and hormonal state also contribute to peak bone mass. Once maximal
skeletal mass is attained, bone resorption slightly exceeds formation,
resulting in age-related bone loss that averages 0.7% per year. Both
sexes are affected equally. Important factors include:
• Age-related changes. Compared to younger individuals, osteoblasts
in older individuals show a reduced proliferative and biosynthetic
capacity and an attenuated response to growth factors, resulting in
a diminished ability to make bone. This form of osteoporosis,
known as senile osteoporosis, is categorized as a “low-turnover” form
of osteoporosis.
• Reduced physical activity. The decreased physical activity sometimes associated with aging results in reduced bone mass. Osteocytes

• Genetic factors. Single-gene defects account for only a small fraction of osteoporosis cases. However, polymorphisms in certain
genes have been linked to osteoporosis by genome-wide association
studies. The most strongly linked genes include RANK, RANKL,
and OPG, all of which encode key osteoclast regulators; the human
leukocyte antigen (HLA) locus (for unknown reasons); and the
estrogen receptor gene (discussed later).
• Calcium nutritional state. Adolescents often have insufficient dietary calcium intake, which can lead to reduced peak bone mass
and increased risk of osteoporosis. Relative calcium deficiency, reduced vitamin D, and elevated PTH levels may also contribute to
development of senile osteoporosis.
• Hormonal influences. Estrogen promotes increased bone density
through a variety of mechanisms, including inhibition of osteoblast apoptosis, stimulation of osteoclast apoptosis, and suppression of RANKL production (see Fig. 26.8). In the decade after
menopause, up to 2% of cortical bone and 9% of cancellous bone
may be lost each year. Estrogen deficiency plays the major role in
this phenomenon, and close to 40% of postmenopausal women
are affected by postmenopausal osteoporosis. Although decreased estrogen increases both bone formation and resorption,
the latter dominates, resulting in high-turnover osteoporosis.
Menopause leads to increased secretion of inflammatory cytokines, such as IL-6, tumor necrosis factor (TNF), and IL-1 by
innate immune cells and IL-17 by Th17 cells in the blood and
marrow through unknown mechanisms. The resulting increases
in RANKL and decreases in OPG stimulate osteoclast recruitment and activity.

decreased in quantity. The entire skeleton is affected in senile and postmenopausal osteoporosis, but certain bones tend to be more severely impacted. Postmenopausal osteoporosis affects mainly bones or portions of
bones that have increased surface area, such as the cancellous compartment
of vertebral bodies The trabecular plates become perforated and thinned and
lose their interconnections, leading to microfractures and eventually to vertebral collapse (Fig. 26.9A). In senile osteoporosis, the cortex is thinned by subperiosteal and endosteal resorption, and the Haversian systems are widened
(Fig. 26.9B).

respond to mechanical load by stimulating or inhibiting osteoblasts and osteoclasts to remodel normal bone. Alterations in the mechanical load sensed by osteocytes underlies localized bone loss in an immobilized or paralyzed extremity, generalized bone loss in the microgravity of outer space, and increased bone density in athletes. The type of exercise is important, as load magnitude influences bone density more than the number of load cycles. Thus, resistance exercises such as weight training are more effective stimuli for increasing bone mass than repetitive endurance activities such as bicycling

• Genetic factors. Single-gene defects account for only a small fraction of osteoporosis cases. However, polymorphisms in certain genes have been linked to osteoporosis by genome-wide association studies. The most strongly linked genes include RANK, RANKL, and OPG, all of which encode key osteoclast regulators; the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) locus (for unknown reasons); and the estrogen receptor gene (discussed later).

• Calcium nutritional state. Adolescents often have insufficient dietary calcium intake, which can lead to reduced peak bone mass and increased risk of osteoporosis. Relative calcium deficiency, reduced vitamin D, and elevated PTH levels may also contribute to development of senile osteoporosis.

• Hormonal influences. Estrogen promotes increased bone density through a variety of mechanisms, including inhibition of osteoblast apoptosis, stimulation of osteoclast apoptosis, and suppression of RANKL production (see Fig. 26.8). In the decade after menopause, up to 2% of cortical bone and 9% of cancellous bone may be lost each year. Estrogen deficiency plays the major role in this phenomenon, and close to 40% of postmenopausal women are affected by postmenopausal osteoporosis. Although decreased estrogen increases both bone formation and resorption, the latter dominates, resulting in high-turnover osteoporosis. Menopause leads to increased secretion of inflammatory cytokines, such as IL-6, tumor necrosis factor (TNF), and IL-1 by innate immune cells and IL-17 by Th17 cells in the blood and marrow through unknown mechanisms. The resulting increases in RANKL and decreases in OPG stimulate osteoclast recruitment and activity. MORPHOLOGY The hallmark of osteoporosis is histologically normal bone that is decreased in quantity. The entire skeleton is affected in senile and postmenopausal osteoporosis, but certain bones tend to be more severely impacted. Postmenopausal osteoporosis affects mainly bones or portions of bones that have increased surface area, such as the cancellous compartment of vertebral bodies The trabecular plates become perforated and thinned and lose their interconnections, leading to microfractures and eventually to vertebral collapse (Fig. 26.9A). In senile osteoporosis, the cortex is thinned by subperiosteal and endosteal resorption, and the Haversian systems are widened (Fig. 26.9B).

Fig. 26.9 Osteoporosis. (A) Osteoporotic vertebral body (right) shortened by compression fractures compared with a normal vertebral body (left). Note that the osteoporotic vertebra has a characteristic loss of horizontal trabeculae and thickened vertical trabeculae. (B) In advanced osteoporosis, both the trabecular bone of the medulla (bottom) and the cortical bone (top) are markedly thinned.

1072 CHAPTER 26 Bones, Joints, and Soft Tissue Tumors
Clinical Features
The clinical manifestations of osteoporosis depend on which bones are
involved. Vertebral fractures in the thoracic and lumbar regions are
painful and when multiple can cause significant loss of height and deformities such as lumbar lordosis and kyphoscoliosis. Fractures of the
femoral neck, pelvis, or spine lead to immobilization and complications such as pulmonary embolism and pneumonia, resulting in over
50,000 deaths per year.
Osteoporosis cannot be reliably detected in plain radiographs until
30% to 40% of the bone mass is lost and blood levels of calcium, phosphorus and alkaline phosphatase are usually normal. Thus, screening
asymptomatic people for osteoporosis is difficult. The best estimates of
bone loss are made using specialized radiographic imaging techniques,
such as dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry and quantitative computed
tomography, both of which measure bone density.
Prevention and treatment of senile and postmenopausal osteoporosis include exercise, appropriate calcium and vitamin D intake, and
pharmacologic agents that reduce bone resorption (particularly
bisphosphonates). Denosumab, an anti-RANKL antibody, has shown
promise in treating some forms of postmenopausal osteoporosis.
Menopausal hormone therapy with estrogen agonists has been used to
slow bone loss and reduce associated fractures, but complications (particularly deep vein thrombosis and stroke) have limited the use of estrogen in the treatment of osteoporosis.
Osteomalacia and Rickets
Osteomalacia and rickets are manifestations of impaired mineralization of bone matrix. Most examples of undermineralized matrix
result from abnormal vitamin D metabolism or vitamin D deficiency
(detailed in Chapter 9). Rickets refers to the disorder in children, in
whom it interferes with the deposition of bone in the growth plates.
Osteomalacia is the adult counterpart, in which bone formed during
remodeling is undermineralized, causing a predisposition to fractures.
Osteomalacia contrasts with osteoporosis, in which mineralization of
bone is normal but bone mass is decreased.
Hyperparathyroidism
In hyperparathyroidism, excess production and activity of parathyroid hormone (PTH) causes increased osteoclast activity, bone resorption, and osteopenia.
Pathogenesis
As discussed in Chapter 24, parathyroid hormone plays a central role
in calcium homeostasis through the following effects.
• Osteoclast activation, which increases bone resorption and calcium
mobilization. PTH mediates this effect indirectly by increasing
RANKL expression on osteoblasts.
• Increased calcium resorption by the renal tubules
• Increased urinary phosphate excretion
• Increased synthesis of active vitamin D, 1,25(OH)₂-D by renal α-1
hydrolase, which in turn increases intestinal calcium absorption
and mobilizes bone calcium by inducing RANKL expression on
osteoblasts
The net result of the above alterations is elevated serum calcium,
which under normal circumstances provides negative feedback to the
parathyroid glands to decrease PTH production. Excessive or inappropriate PTH release may stem from autonomous parathyroid secretion (primary hyperparathyroidism) or may be the result of renal disease
(secondary hyperparathyroidism) (see Chapter 24). In both instances,
hyperparathyroidism produces changes throughout the skeleton due to
unrestrained osteoclast activity. While elevated PTH is responsible for
bone changes in primary hyperparathyroidism, in chronic renal failure
the combination of elevated PTH, inadequate 1,25-(OH)₂- vitamin D
synthesis, hyperphosphatemia, and metabolic acidosis lead to bone
changes as part of a syndrome known as renal osteodystrophy (discussed later). With time, loss of bone mass increases susceptibility to
fractures, bone deformation, and joint problems.
MORPHOLOGY
Symptomatic, untreated primary hyperparathyroidism manifests with three interrelated skeletal abnormalities: osteoporosis, brown tumors, and osteitis fibrosa
cystica. Osteoporosis is generalized but is most severe in the phalanges, vertebrae, and proximal femur. Hyperparathyroidism most prominently enhances osteoclast activity within cortical bone (subperiosteal and endosteal surfaces), but
cancellous bone can also be affected. At these sites, osteoclasts may tunnel into
and dissect centrally along the length of the trabeculae, leaving adjacent marrow
spaces to be replaced by fibrovascular tissue. This creates a railroad track-like
appearance that is referred to as dissecting osteitis (Fig. 26.10A), a misnomer
as this is not an inflammatory lesion. Radiographs show decreased bone density.
Bone loss in hyperparathyroidism may lead to microfractures, secondary
hemorrhage, macrophage recruitment, and ingrowth of reparative fibrous tissue to create a mass lesion called brown tumor (Fig. 26.10B). The brown color
reflects vascularity, hemorrhage, and hemosiderin. Brown tumors often undergo cystic degeneration. The combination of increased bone cell activity,
peritrabecular fibrosis, and cystic brown tumors is the hallmark of severe hyperparathyroidism and is known as generalized osteitis fibrosa cystica
(von Recklinghausen disease of bone).
Fig. 26.10 Hyperparathyroidism. (A) Osteoclasts boring into the center
of the trabecula producing a “railroad track” appearance (dissecting
osteitis). (B) Resected rib, harboring an expansile brown tumor adjacent
to the costal cartilage.

Clinical Features

The clinical manifestations of osteoporosis depend on which bones are involved. Vertebral fractures in the thoracic and lumbar regions are painful and when multiple can cause significant loss of height and deformities such as lumbar lordosis and kyphoscoliosis. Fractures of the femoral neck, pelvis, or spine lead to immobilization and complications such as pulmonary embolism and pneumonia, resulting in over 50,000 deaths per year.

Osteoporosis cannot be reliably detected in plain radiographs until 30% to 40% of the bone mass is lost and blood levels of calcium, phosphorus and alkaline phosphatase are usually normal. Thus, screening asymptomatic people for osteoporosis is difficult. The best estimates of bone loss are made using specialized radiographic imaging techniques, such as dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry and quantitative computed tomography, both of which measure bone density.

Prevention and treatment of senile and postmenopausal osteoporosis include exercise, appropriate calcium and vitamin D intake, and pharmacologic agents that reduce bone resorption (particularly bisphosphonates). Denosumab, an anti-RANKL antibody, has shown promise in treating some forms of postmenopausal osteoporosis. Menopausal hormone therapy with estrogen agonists has been used to slow bone loss and reduce associated fractures, but complications (particularly deep vein thrombosis and stroke) have limited the use of estrogen in the treatment of osteoporosis. Osteomalacia and Rickets Osteomalacia and rickets are manifestations of impaired mineralization of bone matrix. Most examples of undermineralized matrix result from abnormal vitamin D metabolism or vitamin D deficiency (detailed in Chapter 9). Rickets refers to the disorder in children, in whom it interferes with the deposition of bone in the growth plates. Osteomalacia is the adult counterpart, in which bone formed during remodeling is undermineralized, causing a predisposition to fractures. Osteomalacia contrasts with osteoporosis, in which mineralization of bone is normal but bone mass is decreased.
Hyperparathyroidism

In hyperparathyroidism, excess production and activity of parathyroid hormone (PTH) causes increased osteoclast activity, bone resorption, and osteopenia. Pathogenesis As discussed in Chapter 24, parathyroid hormone plays a central role in calcium homeostasis through the following effects.
• Osteoclast activation, which increases bone resorption and calcium mobilization. PTH mediates this effect indirectly by increasing RANKL expression on osteoblasts.
• Increased calcium resorption by the renal tubules
• Increased urinary phosphate excretion

• Increased synthesis of active vitamin D, 1,25(OH)₂-D by renal α-1 hydrolase, which in turn increases intestinal calcium absorption and mobilizes bone calcium by inducing RANKL expression on osteoblasts The net result of the above alterations is elevated serum calcium, which under normal circumstances provides negative feedback to the parathyroid glands to decrease PTH production. Excessive or inappropriate PTH release may stem from autonomous parathyroid secretion (primary hyperparathyroidism) or may be the result of renal disease (secondary hyperparathyroidism) (see Chapter 24). In both instances, hyperparathyroidism produces changes throughout the skeleton due to unrestrained osteoclast activity. While elevated PTH is responsible for bone changes in primary hyperparathyroidism, in chronic renal failure the combination of elevated PTH, inadequate 1,25-(OH)₂- vitamin D synthesis, hyperphosphatemia, and metabolic acidosis lead to bone changes as part of a syndrome known as renal osteodystrophy (discussed later). With time, loss of bone mass increases susceptibility to fractures, bone deformation, and joint problems.
MORPHOLOGY

Symptomatic, untreated primary hyperparathyroidism manifests with three interrelated skeletal abnormalities: osteoporosis, brown tumors, and osteitis fibrosa cystica. Osteoporosis is generalized but is most severe in the phalanges, vertebrae, and proximal femur. Hyperparathyroidism most prominently enhances osteoclast activity within cortical bone (subperiosteal and endosteal surfaces), but cancellous bone can also be affected. At these sites, osteoclasts may tunnel into and dissect centrally along the length of the trabeculae, leaving adjacent marrow spaces to be replaced by fibrovascular tissue. This creates a railroad track-like appearance that is referred to as dissecting osteitis (Fig. 26.10A), a misnomer as this is not an inflammatory lesion. Radiographs show decreased bone density. Bone loss in hyperparathyroidism may lead to microfractures, secondary hemorrhage, macrophage recruitment, and ingrowth of reparative fibrous tissue to create a mass lesion called brown tumor (Fig. 26.10B). The brown color reflects vascularity, hemorrhage, and hemosiderin. Brown tumors often undergo cystic degeneration. The combination of increased bone cell activity, peritrabecular fibrosis, and cystic brown tumors is the hallmark of severe hyperparathyroidism and is known as generalized osteitis fibrosa cystica (von Recklinghausen disease of bone).

CHAPTER 26
Clinical Features
As bone mass decreases, affected patients are increasingly suscepti-
ble to fractures, bone deformation, and joint problems. Osteitis fi-
brosa cystica is now uncommon because hyperparathyroidism is
usually diagnosed on routine blood tests and treated at an early
stage. In symptomatic patients, surgical removal of autonomously
functioning parathyroid glands (typically due to involvement by
parathyroid adenoma; Chapter 24) can completely reverse the bone
changes. Secondary hyperparathyroidism can cause similar changes,
but the process is usually less severe and less prolonged, so skeletal
abnormalities tend to be milder. Asymptomatic cases are followed
by  monitoring  serum  calcium  and  creatinine  and  bone  mineral
density.
Renal Osteodystrophy
The term renal osteodystrophy describes the collective skeletal
changes that occur in chronic renal disease, including those as-
sociated with dialysis. The manifestations include many of the enti-
ties described earlier, including (1) osteopenia/osteoporosis, (2) os-
teomalacia,  (3)  secondary  hyperparathyroidism,  and  (4)  growth
retardation in skeletally immature patients. As medical advances
have prolonged the lives of individuals with renal disease, the im-
pact of abnormal renal function on skeletal homeostasis has as-
sumed greater clinical importance. Histologic bone changes in indi-
viduals with end-stage renal failure can be divided into three major
types of disorders:
•  High-turnover osteodystrophy is characterized by increased bone
resorption and bone formation, with the former predominating.
•  Low-turnover or aplastic disease is manifested by adynamic bone
(little osteoclastic and osteoblastic activity) and, less commonly,
osteomalacia.
•  Mixed pattern disease is heterogeneous, with areas of high turnover
and low turnover.
Pathogenesis
Kidney disease causes skeletal abnormalities through several interre-
lated mechanisms (Fig. 26.11):
•  Tubular  dysfunction,  leading  to  tubular  and  systemic  acidosis.
Acidosis in turn leads to increased expression of RANKL on osteo-
blasts and increased osteoclast activity, resulting in matrix resorp-
tion and osteopenia.

KEY CONCEPTS
Metabolic Diseases of Bone
•  Osteopenia and osteoporosis are conditions in which bone is normally
mineralized but decreased in quantity. Osteoporosis is defined as bone loss
sufficient to increase fracture risk and is associated with significant morbid-
ity and mortality from fractures. Multiple factors including peak bone mass,
age, physical activity, genetics, nutrition, and hormonal influences contrib-
ute to its pathogenesis.
•  Osteomalacia is defined by the presence of bone that is insufficiently min-
eralized. In the developing skeleton, this results in rickets.
•  Hyperparathyroidism arises from either autonomous or compensatory hy-
persecretion of PTH and can lead to osteoporosis, brown tumors, and oste-
itis fibrosa cystica. In high-income countries where early diagnosis is the
norm, these manifestations are rare.
•  Renal osteodystrophy is marked by a constellation of bone abnormalities
(osteopenia, osteomalacia, hyperparathyroidism, and growth retardation)
that occur because of chronic renal failure. The bone changes stem from
decreased tubular, glomerular, and hormonal renal functions.
Paget Disease of Bone (Osteitis Deformans)
Paget disease of bone is a disorder associated with increased but
disordered and structurally abnormal bone formation. It develops
in three sequential phases: (1) an initial osteolytic stage; (2) a mixed
osteoclastic-osteoblastic stage, which ends with a predominance of
osteoclastic activity; and (3) a final burned-out, quiescent, osteoscle-
rotic stage (Fig. 26.12).
Paget disease usually presents in late adulthood and becomes pro-
gressively more common with increasing age. An estimated 1% of the
US population older than age 40 years is affected. The exact incidence
is  unknown  because  many  affected  individuals  are  asymptomatic.
Paget disease is relatively common in the United Kingdom, central
Europe, and Greece as well as areas colonized by European immigrants
(e.g., the United States and Australia). By contrast, Paget disease is rare
in native populations of Scandinavia, China, Japan, and Africa. A de-
crease in new cases has been observed in some countries over the past
30 years.
Pathogenesis
The cause of Paget disease remains uncertain but current evidence sug-
gests both genetic and environmental contributions. Approximately
60% of cases of familial Paget disease and 10% of sporadic cases are
associated with germline mutations in the SQSTM1 gene, which en-
codes a protein known as sequestosome-1. Mutations in SQSTM1
appear to lead to increased NF-κB activity and thus increase osteoclast
activity. Activating mutations in the RANK gene and inactivating mu-
tations in the OPG gene account for some cases of juvenile Paget dis-
ease. The geographic variation in the incidence of the disease suggests
involvement of an environmental factor that remains unknown. In
vitro studies have raised the possibility that chronic infection of osteo-
clast precursors by measles or other RNA viruses may play a role, but
firm links to the disease have yet to be established.

common pathologic conditions affecting bone. The following qualifiers
describe fracture types and affect treatment:
• Simple: the overlying skin is intact
• Compound: the bone communicates with the skin surface
• Comminuted: the bone is fragmented
• Displaced: the ends of the bone at the fracture site are not aligned
• Stress: a slowly developing fracture that follows a period of increased
physical activity in which the bone is subjected to repetitive
loads
• Greenstick: extending only partially through the bone; these fractures
are common in infants and young children whose bones are
soft
• Pathologic: involving bone weakened by an underlying disease process,
such as a tumor
Healing of Fractures
Bone has a remarkable capacity for repair. At the time of fracture, rupture
of blood vessels results in a hematoma that fills and surrounds the
area of injury ( Fig. 26.14 ). The clotted blood seals off the fracture site
and provides a fibrin scaffold that guides the influx of inflammatory
cells and ingrowth of fibroblasts and new capillaries. Simultaneously,
degranulated platelets and migrating inflammatory cells release PDGF,
TGF-β , FGF, and other growth factors that activate osteoprogenitor
cells in the periosteum, medullary cavity, and surrounding soft tissues
and stimulate osteoclastic and osteoblastic activity. By the end of the
first week, a mass of predominantly uncalcified tissue, called soft callus
or procallus , bridges the ends of the fractured bones providing some
anchorage but not structural rigidity for weight bearing. By approximately
2 weeks after injury, the procallus is converted into a bony callus
by the deposition of woven bone. The activated osteoprogenitor cells
deposit subperiosteal trabeculae of woven bone oriented perpendicular
to the cortical axis within the medullary cavity. In some cases,
activated soft tissue mesenchymal cells may also differentiate into
chondrocytes that produce fibrocartilage and hyaline cartilage. The
cartilage then undergoes endochondral ossification, forming new
bone. As a result, fractured bone ends are bridged and with progressive
mineralization, the stiffness and strength of the callus increases to
allow weight bearing.
In the early stages of callus formation, excess fibrous tissue,
cartilage, and woven bone is produced. As the callus matures and
is subjected to weight-bearing forces, portions that are not physically
stressed are resorbed. This remodeling reduces the size of the
callus until the shape and outline of the fractured bone are reestablished
as lamellar bone. The healing process is completed by restoration
of the medullary cavity. In simple fractures with adequate
immobilization and absent comorbidities, near-perfect union is
the norm.
The healing of a fracture may be impeded by several factors.
• Displaced and comminuted fractures frequently result in some deformity.
• Bone neoplasms (primary or metastatic) that produce a pathologic
fracture often inhibit the normal healing process.
• Inadequate immobilization permits movement of the callus and interferes
with normal maturation, which may result in delayed union
or nonunion. If nonunion persists, the malformed callus undergoes
cystic degeneration and the luminal surface can become lined by

1076 CHAPTER 26 Bones, Joints, and Soft Tissue Tumors
OSTEONECROSIS (AVASCULAR NECROSIS)
Osteonecrosis refers to infarction (ischemic necrosis) of bone and marrow.
A diverse set of conditions predispose to bone ischemia, including
vascular injury (trauma, vasculitis), drugs (e.g., corticosteroids, bisphos-phosphonates), systemic disease (e.g., sickle cell crisis), and radiation.
Osteonecrosis of the jaw is a rare complication of long term treatment of
osteoporosis.with bisphophonates. In about 25% of cases the cause is
unknown (idiopathic). Mechanisms of avascular necrosis include mechanical disruption of vessels (e.g., fracture), thrombotic occlusion, and
extravascular compression. Osteonecrosis peaks in middle adulthood and
accounts for about 10% of hip arthroplasties in the United States.
MORPHOLOGY
Bone infarcts may be medullary or subchondral. Regardless of etiology, medullary infarcts are geographic in shape and involve both trabecular bone and
marrow but spare the cortex, which is protected by collateral blood flow from
the periosteum. In subchondral infarcts, a triangular segment with subchondral
bone plate at its base undergoes necrosis; the overlying articular cartilage remains viable due to nutrients within synovial fluid. Dead bone is recognized
histologically by empty lacunae lacking osteocytes. The marrow fat contains
necrotic adipocytes. The released fatty acids bind calcium and form insoluble
calcium soaps. The remaining trabeculae act as scaffolding for deposition of
new bone, while osteoclasts resorb necrotic trabeculae. The pace of repair in
subchondral infarcts is slow, resulting in collapse and fracturing of the necrotic
bone and sloughing of the articular cartilage (Fig. 26.15).
Clinical Features
Symptoms depend on location and extent of infarct. Typically, subchondral infarcts cause pain that is initially associated with activity but
becomes constant as secondary changes supervene. As mentioned
above, subchondral infarcts often collapse, resulting in severe secondary osteoarthritis. Treatment ranges from conservative measures (limiting weight-bearing activities, immobilization) to surgery. Medullary
infarcts are usually small and clinically silent.
OSTEOMYELITIS
Osteomyelitis is bone and marrow inflammation, virtually always
secondary to infection. Osteomyelitis may be a complication of any
systemic infection but frequently manifests as a solitary primary focus.
Fig. 26.15 Osteonecrosis. Femoral head with a subchondral, triangle-shaped pale area of necrotic bone (arrow). The space between the
overlying articular cartilage and bone is caused by trabecular compression fractures without repair.
All types of organisms, including viruses, parasites, fungi, and bacteria,
can produce osteomyelitis, but certain pyogenic bacteria and mycobacteria are the most common causes.
Pyogenic Osteomyelitis
Pyogenic osteomyelitis is almost always caused by bacterial infection.
Organisms may reach the bone by (1) hematogenous spread, (2) extension from a contiguous site, or (3) direct implantation after compound
fracture or orthopedic procedures. In otherwise healthy children, most
osteomyelitis is hematogenous in origin and is more common in long
bones. The initiating bacteremia may stem from seemingly trivial mucosal injuries or from minor skin infections. In adults, osteomyelitis is
most often a complication of open fractures, surgical procedures, or
diabetes, which predisposes to infections of the feet. Osteomyelitis is
particularly worrisome in infants, in whom epiphyseal infection can
spread to a joint, resulting in septic or suppurative arthritis, articular
cartilage destruction, and permanent disability.
Causative pathogens vary depending on the anatomic location and
clinical setting. Staphylococcus aureus is responsible for 80% to 90% of
culture-positive pyogenic osteomyelitis. Staphylococcal cell wall proteins bind to bone matrix components such as collagen, facilitating
bacterial adherence to bone. In the neonatal period, group B streptococci and E. coli are likely pathogens, whereas in older children gram-positive organisms such as S. aureus are the most likely cause. Mixed
bacterial infections are common in the setting of direct spread, surgery,
or open fractures. In patients with sickle cell anemia, areas of osteonecrosis serve as a nidus of bacterial seeding and loss of splenic function
impairs the immune response; in this setting, Salmonella and other
gram-negative organisms are the most frequent pathogens. Microbio-logical cultures are obtained whenever possible to identify the causative
organism. Specific organisms are only identified in approximately 50%
of patients; it is hoped that introduction of sensitive PCR assays that
identify microbe-specific DNA sequences will increase this number.
The location of bone infections is influenced by the osseous vascular circulation, which varies with age. In neonates, metaphyseal vessels
penetrate the growth plate, resulting in frequent infection of the metaphysis, epiphysis, or both. In older children, involvement of the metaphysis is typical. The epiphyses and subchondral regions are more
commonly involved in adults after growth plate closure, which creates
anastomoses between metaphyseal and epiphyseal vessels that provide
a route for bacterial spread.
MORPHOLOGY
Changes associated with osteomyelitis depend on the stage (acute, subacute,
and chronic) and location of the infection. In the acute phase, bacteria proliferate
and induce a neutrophilic reaction. Necrosis of bone cells and marrow ensues
within 48 hours. Bacteria and the associated inflammatory response then spread
through the Haversian canals to reach the periosteum. Because the periosteum
is loosely attached to the cortex in children, subperiosteal abscesses may dissect
along the bone surface. Lifting of the periosteum further impairs blood supply
and contributes to the necrosis. Soft tissue abscesses may also form after periosteal rupture and may channel to the skin as draining sinuses.
As the inflammatory process evolves during the first week, chronic inflammatory cells are recruited that release cytokines that stimulate bone resorption,
fibrous tissue ingrowth, and deposition of reactive bone at the periphery of the
infection. The dead bone is known as sequestrum. The new reactive bone can
form a shell of living tissue known as involucrum around the devitalized, infected bone (Fig. 26.16). The histologic findings of chronic osteomyelitis are
more variable but typically involve marrow fibrosis, sequestrum, and a chronic
inflammatory infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells.

Clinical Features

Hematogenous osteomyelitis may present acutely as a systemic illness with malaise, fever, chills, leukocytosis, and intense throbbing pain over the affected region. In other instances, the presentation is subtle, with only unexplained fever (infants) or localized pain (adults). Plain radiographs characteristically show a lytic focus of bone destruction and associated reactive bone; MRI is more specific and sensitive for identifying the changes of osteomyelitis. Biopsy and microbial culture are required to identify the pathogen in most instances.
The combination of antibiotics and surgical drainage is usually curative, but in 5% to 25% of cases acute osteomyelitis fails to resolve.

This unfavorable outcome is particularly likely in the setting of delayed diagnosis, extensive bone necrosis, inadequate antibiotic treatment  or  surgical  debridement,  or  weakened  host  immunity.  The

course of such chronic infections may be punctuated by spontaneous flares  that  may  occur  after  years  of  dormancy.  Complications  of chronic osteomyelitis include pathologic fracture, secondary (r eactive) amyloidosis, endocarditis, sepsis, and the development of squamous cell carcinoma in draining sinus tracts or sarcoma in the infected bone.
Mycobacterial Osteomyelitis

Mycobacterial  osteomyelitis  tends  to  be  more  destructive  and resistant  to  control  than  pyogenic  osteomyelitis.  Mycobacterial osteomyelitis was previously limited to lower resource countries, but the incidence has risen worldwide due to immigration and increased numbers  of  immunocompromised  individuals.  Overall,  approximately 1% to 3% of individuals with pulmonary or extrapulmonary tuberculosis develop osseous infection, which may be present for years prior to diagnosis. The typical patient presents with localized pain,  low-grade  fever,  chills,  or  weight  loss.  Infection  is  usually solitary in immunocompetent patients but can disseminate in the immunocompromised.

Mycobacteria that infect bone are usually bloodborne and originate from a focus of active visceral disease elsewhere. Direct extension (e.g., from a pulmonary focus into a rib or from tracheobronchial nodes into adjacent vertebrae) may also occur. The principal histologic feature, the presence of caseating granulomas typical of other involved sites, is also seen in tuberculous osteomyelitis. Mycobacterial osteomyelitis Bones, Joints, and Soft Tissue Tumors 1077
tends to be more destructive and resistant to control than pyogenic osteomyelitis.
The spine is involved in 40% of mycobacterial osteomyelitis cases
(Pott disease). Infection often tracks through intervertebral discs to involve multiple vertebrae and surrounding soft tissues (Fig. 26.17).

Discs and vertebral destruction result in permanent compression fractures that produce scoliosis, kyphosis, and neurologic deficits secondary to spinal cord and nerve compression. Tuberculous osteomyelitis
may also cause tuberculous arthritis, sinus tract formation, abscesses, and amyloidosis.
Skeletal Syphilis

Syphilis (Treponema pallidum) and yaws (Treponema pertenue) can involve bone. Although the incidence of syphilis is increasing, bone involvement remains rare because diagnosis and treatment typically occur before bone disease can develop.

In congenital syphilis, bone lesions appear in the fifth month of gestation and are fully developed at birth. The spirochetes concentrate at sites of active endochondral ossification and within the periosteum to cause osteochondritis and periostitis, respectively. The characteristic saber shin is produced by reactive periosteal bone deposition on the medial and anterior surfaces of the tibia.

In acquired syphilis, bone disease begins early in the tertiary stage, usually 2 to 5 years after the initial infection. Bones of the nose, palate, skull, and extremities, especially the long tubular bones such as the tibia, are involved most frequently.

1078 CHAPTER 26 Bones, Joints, and Soft Tissue Tumors
MORPHOLOGY
Spirochetes can be detected with silver stains or by immunohistochemistry.
Edematous granulation tissue with numerous plasma cells and necrotic bone
characterizes syphilitic bone disease. Obliterative endarteritis typically accompanies caseous necrosis as part of gummas, which may be present in
congenital or acquired syphilis (Chapter 8).
BONE TUMORS
Primary bone tumors are rare and are vastly outnumbered by metastases and hematopoietic tumors in the marrow. Nevertheless, mortality is high for many of these neoplasms and disfiguring surgery is
often required for treatment, making management of bone malignancies challenging. Therapy for the ,2400 new bone sarcomas diagnosed each year in the United States aims to optimize survival and
maintain function of a ffected body parts.
The predilection of specific types of tumors to affect certain age
groups and particular anatomic sites provides a diagnostic clue. For
example, osteosarcoma incidence peaks during adolescence and most
frequently involves the distal femur and proximal tibia. By contrast,
chondrosarcoma affects older adults and arises in the pelvic bones and
proximal extremities.
Bone tumors may present in a variety of ways. Benign lesions are
often asymptomatic incidental findings while malignant tumors cause
pain, a growing mass, or pathologic fractures. Radiologic imaging defines tumor location and extent and can identify features that narrow
the differential diagnosis, but biopsy is necessary for definitive diagnosis in almost all cases.
Bone tumors are classified according to the normal cell types they
recapitulate or matrix they produce. Lesions that do not have normal
tissue counterparts are grouped according to clinicopathologic
features (Table 26.4). Benign tumors greatly outnumber malignant
tumors in incidence and occur with greatest frequency during the first
3 decades of life. In older adults, a bone tumor is more likely to be
malignant.
Bone-Forming Tumors
Tumors in this category produce unmineralized osteoid or mineralized
woven bone.
Osteoid Osteoma and Osteoblastoma
Osteoid osteoma and osteoblastoma are benign bone-producing
tumors with similar histologic appearances but different clinical
and radiographical features. By definition, osteoid osteomas are less
than 2 cm in diameter. They are most common in young males.
About 50% of cases involve the cortex of the femur or tibia. A thick
rim of reactive cortical bone may be the only radiographic clue.
Despite their small size, osteoid osteomas present with severe nocturnal pain that is probably caused by prostaglandin E₂ (PGE₂) produced by the proliferating osteoblasts and is relieved by aspirin and
other nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Osteoblasto-mas are larger than 2 cm, typically involve the posterior components
of the vertebrae (laminae and pedicles), cause pain that is unresponsive to aspirin, and usually do not induce reactive cortical bone.
Osteoid osteoma can be treated by radiofrequency ablation, but osteoblastoma usually requires curettage or en bloc excision. Malignant
transformation is rare.

Modified from Unni KK, Inwards CY. Dahlin’s Bone Tumors. 6th ed. Lippincott-Williams & Wilkins; 2010:5.

CHAPTER 26 Bones, Joints, and Soft Tissue Tumors 1079
MORPHOLOGY
Osteoid osteoma and osteoblastoma are round-to-oval masses of hemorrhagic,
gritty tan tissue. They are well circumscribed and composed of delicate interconnected trabeculae of woven bone rimmed by a single layer of prominent
osteoblasts (Fig. 26.18A) and surrounded by loose connective tissue with many
dilated and congested capillaries. Reactive bone encircles the actual neoplasm, or nidus, which forms a small radiolucent core that may be centrally
mineralized (Fig. 26.18B). The relatively small size, well-defined margins, and
benign cytomorphology of the neoplastic osteoblasts help distinguish these
tumors from osteosarcoma.
Osteosarcoma
Osteosarcoma is a malignant tumor that produces osteoid matrix or
mineralized bone. Excluding hematopoietic tumors, osteosarcoma is
the most common primary malignant tumor of bone. The age distribution of osteosarcoma is bimodal, with 75% occurring before 20 years
of age. A second smaller peak occurs in older adults, in whom it is
frequently associated with predisposing conditions (secondary osteosarcoma) such as Paget disease of bone, bone infarcts, and chronic osteomyelitis. Males are affected slightly more often than females (1.6:1).
Although any bone can be involved, tumors usually arise in the metaphyseal region of the long bones; almost 50% are near the knee in the
distal femur or proximal tibia.
Osteosarcoma often presents as a painful, progressively enlarging
mass, sometimes with a pathologic fracture. Radiographically, the enlarging tumor forms a destructive, mixed lytic and sclerotic mass with
infiltrative margins (Fig. 26.19A). The tumor frequently breaks through
the cortex and lifts the periosteum, inducing reactive periosteal bone
formation. The triangular shadow between the cortex and raised periosteal ends, known radiographically as Codman’ triangle, indicates an
aggressive tumor.
Pathogenesis
The peak incidence of osteosarcoma is during the adolescent growth
spurt. The tumor occurs most frequently in the growth plate of rapidly
growing bones, where increased proliferation may predispose to mutations that drive oncogenesis. Osteosarcomas typically have complex
karyotypes with numerous chromosomal aberrations and mutations in
well-known tumor suppressor genes and oncogenes (Chapter 7),
including:
• RB mutations are present in up to 70% of sporadic osteosarcomas
and germline RB mutations confer a 1000-fold increased risk of
osteosarcoma.
• TP53 is mutated in the germline of individuals with Li-Fraumeni
syndrome, who have a greatly increased incidence of osteosarcoma. Inactivating mutations in TP53 are common in sporadic
osteosarcomas.
• CDKN2A, which encodes two tumor suppressors, p16 and p14, is
inactivated in many osteosarcomas.
• MDM2 and CDK4, which inhibit p53 and RB function, respectively, are overexpressed in many low-grade osteosarcomas, often
through amplification of these genes on chromosome 12q14.
• MYC amplification is seen in up to half of osteosarcomas and may
be associated with a particularly poor prognosis.
MORPHOLOGY
Osteosarcomas are large, gritty, gray-white tumors that often contain hemorrhage and cystic degeneration (Fig. 26.19B). The tumor frequently destroys the
surrounding cortices to produce a soft tissue mass, spreads extensively in the
medullary canal, and replaces hematopoietic marrow. Tumors infrequently
penetrate the epiphyseal plate or enter the joint, where they may grow along
tendoligamentous structures or through the attachment site of the joint capsule.
Osteosarcomas demonstrate pleomorphism, large hyperchromatic nuclei,
bizarre tumor giant cells, and abundant mitoses, including abnormal (e.g.,
tripolar) forms. Extensive necrosis and intravascular invasion are also common.
Diagnosis requires the presence of malignant tumor cells producing
unmineralized osteoid or mineralized bone (Fig. 26.20), which is typically
fine and lacelike, but can also form broad sheets or primitive trabeculae. In
some cases, malignant cells also produce cartilage; if abundant, such tumors
are classified as chondroblastic osteosarcoma.
Clinical Features
Osteosarcomas are generally assumed to have occult metastases at the
time of diagnosis. As a result, treatment typically consists of neoadjuvant chemotherapy, surgery, and postoperative adjuvant chemotherapy. Chemotherapy has greatly improved osteosarcoma prognosis,

Cartilage-Forming Tumors
These tumors are characterized by the formation of hyaline cartilage by neoplastic cells. Benign cartilage tumors are much more common than malignant lesions. Together, cartilage-forming tumors
account for most primary nonhematopoietic bone tumors.
Osteochondroma
Osteochondroma, or exostosis, is a benign cartilage-capped tumor
that arises from the bone surface. It may be sessile or pedunculated
with a bony stalk. About 85% of osteochondromas are solitary and
sporadic. The remainder occur as part of autosomal dominant multiple
hereditary exostosis syndrome (described later). Solitary osteochondromas are usually diagnosed in late adolescence and early adulthood,
whereas multiple hereditary exostosis syndrome becomes apparent
during childhood. In those with sporadic disease, males are affected
three times more often than females. Osteochondromas develop only
in bones of endochondral origin. The most common site is the metaphysis near the growth plate of long tubular bones, especially near
the knee, followed by the bones of the pelvis, scapula, and ribs, where
they tend to have short stalks.
Osteochondromas present as slow-growing masses, which can be
painful if they impinge on a nerve or if the stalk is fractured. In many
cases, they are detected incidentally. In multiple hereditary exostosis
syndrome, the underlying bones may be bowed and shortened, reflecting an associated disturbance in epiphyseal growth.
Pathogenesis
Hereditary exostoses are associated with germline mutations in the
EXT1 or EXT2 genes and subsequent loss of the remaining wild-type
allele in chondrocytes of the growth plate. (Fig. 26.21A). Most
mutations result in a truncated or nonfunctional protein. Reduced
expression of EXT1 or EXT2 has also been observed in sporadic osteochondromas. These genes encode glycosyltransferases involved in
heparan sulfate biosynthesis. Loss of heparan sulfate may allow mutated chondrocyte progenitors in the growth plate to proliferate and
lose polarity, leading to secondary perturbation of signaling through
the Hedgehog, BMP, FGFR3, and Wnt signaling pathways.

MORPHOLOGY
Osteochondromas are sessile or pedunculated and range in size from 1 to
20 cm. The cortex of the stalk merges with the cortex of the host bone, so
that the medullary cavity of the osteochondroma is in continuity with that
of the bone from which it arises (Fig. 26.21B). On plain radiographs the cap
is oriented away from the nearest physis. The cap is composed of benign
hyaline cartilage (Fig. 26.21C) and is covered by perichondrium. The cartilage has the histologic appearance of a disorganized growth plate and undergoes endochondral ossification, with newly made bone forming the inner
portion of the head and stalk. Osteochondromas in multiple hereditary exostoses syndrome are sometimes more cellular and display more atypia
than the sporadic variety.
Clinical Features
Osteochondromas usually stop expanding at the time of growth plate
closure and, when symptomatic, are cured by simple excision. Secondary chondrosarcoma occurs rarely, usually in tumors associated with
multiple hereditary exostosis.

bones of endochondral origin. Tumors can arise within the medullary cavity (enchondroma) or on the bone surface (juxtacortical
chondroma). Enchondroma is the most common cartilage-producing tumor. It typically presents as a solitary metaphyseal

and Maffucci syndrome are nonhereditary disorders characterized by multiple enchondromas (enchondromatosis). Maffucci
syndrome is distinguished from Ollier disease by also being associated with spindle cell hemangiomas and other noncartilage

Enchondromas are most often diagnosed between 20 and 50 years
of age. When they involve large bones, they are usually asymptomatic
and detected incidentally. Occasionally, they may be painful or cause
pathologic fractures. In enchondromatosis, the tumors may be numerous and large, producing severe deformities.
Pathogenesis
Heterozygous mutations in the IDH1 and IDH2 genes, which encode
two isoforms of the isocitrate dehydrogenase enzyme, are present in
most enchondromas. Individuals with enchondromatosis syndromes
are genetically mosaic, harboring IDH mutations in a subset of otherwise normal cells throughout their bodies. Similarly, IDH mutations are present in only a subset of tumor cells in syndromic and
sporadic enchondromas. The IDH mutations cause the encoded
proteins to acquire a new enzymatic activity that leads to the synthesis of 2-hydroxyglutarate. As discussed in Chapter 7, this “oncometabolite” interferes with regulation of DNA methylation, an effect
that likely alters the expression of several genes that regulate differentiation, cell growth, and survival. Of note, excessive 2-hydroxyglutarate promotes differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells toward the
chondrocyte lineage.
MORPHOLOGY
Enchondromas are well-circumscribed nodules that are usually smaller than
3 cm, gray-blue, and translucent. Histologically, enchondromas are composed of hyaline cartilage containing cytologically benign chondrocytes
(Fig. 26.22B). Peripheral endochondral ossification may occur, and the center can calcify and infarct. The enchondromas in Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome are sometimes more cellular and display more atypia than
sporadic enchondromas.
Clinical Features
The growth potential of enchondromas is limited. Treatment depends
on the clinical situation and if necessary, usually consists of curettage.
Solitary chondromas rarely undergo sarcomatous transformation, but
those associated with enchondromatosis do so more frequently. Individuals with Maffucci syndrome develop multiple enchondromas and
spindle cell hemangiomas and are also at risk of developing other
malignancies, including brain gliomas, another type of cancer associated with IDH gene mutations (Chapter 28).
Chondrosarcoma
Chondrosarcomas are malignant tumors that produce cartilage.
After osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma is the second most common
malignant matrix-producing tumor of bone. These tumors are subclassified into hyaline cartilage-producing (conventional), clear cell, dedifferentiated, and mesenchymal subtypes.
Conventional chondrosarcomas represent approximately 90% of
all chondrosarcomas and arise in individuals in their fourth decade or
older. Men are affected twice as frequently as women. Conventional
chondrosarcomas commonly arise in the axial skeleton, especially the
pelvis, shoulder, and ribs, but unlike benign enchondroma, distal extremities are rarely involved. About 15% of conventional chondrosarcomas are secondary and arise from preexisting enchondromas or
osteochondromas. On imaging, the calcified matrix of chondrosarcomas appears as foci of flocculent densities. Slow-growing low-grade
tumors cause reactive cortical thickening, whereas aggressive
high-grade neoplasms destroy the cortex and form soft tissue masses
(Fig. 26.23A).
The clear cell and mesenchymal variants occur in younger people
in their teens or 20s. The clear cell variant is unique in that it originates
in the epiphyses of long tubular bones.
Pathogenesis
Although chondrosarcomas are genetically heterogeneous, a few recurrent driver mutations are recognized. Chondrosarcomas arising in
multiple osteochondroma syndrome exhibit mutations in the EXT1 or
EXT2 genes that regulate the synthesis of cartilaginous matrix proteins. Both chondromatosis-related and sporadic chondrosarcomas
may have IDH1 or IDH2 mutations. Silencing of the CDKN2A tumor
suppressor locus by DNA methylation is common in sporadic tumors.

Enchondromas are most often diagnosed between 20 and 50 years of age. When they involve large bones, they are usually asymptomatic and detected incidentally. Occasionally, they may be painful or cause pathologic fractures. In enchondromatosis, the tumors may be numerous and large, producing severe deformities. Pathogenesis Heterozygous mutations in the IDH1 and IDH2 genes, which encode two isoforms of the isocitrate dehydrogenase enzyme, are present in most enchondromas. Individuals with enchondromatosis syndromes are genetically mosaic, harboring IDH mutations in a subset of otherwise normal cells throughout their bodies. Similarly, IDH mutations are present in only a subset of tumor cells in syndromic and sporadic enchondromas. The IDH mutations cause the encoded proteins to acquire a new enzymatic activity that leads to the synthesis of 2-hydroxyglutarate. As discussed in Chapter 7, this “oncometabolite” interferes with regulation of DNA methylation, an effect that likely alters the expression of several genes that regulate differentiation, cell growth, and survival. Of note, excessive 2-hydroxyglutarate promotes differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells toward the chondrocyte lineage.

MORPHOLOGY

Enchondromas are well-circumscribed nodules that are usually smaller than 3 cm, gray-blue, and translucent. Histologically, enchondromas are composed of hyaline cartilage containing cytologically benign chondrocytes (Fig. 26.22B). Peripheral endochondral ossification may occur, and the center can calcify and infarct. The enchondromas in Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome are sometimes more cellular and display more atypia than sporadic enchondromas.

Clinical Features

The growth potential of enchondromas is limited. Treatment depends on the clinical situation and if necessary, usually consists of curettage. Solitary chondromas rarely undergo sarcomatous transformation, but those associated with enchondromatosis do so more frequently. Individuals with Maffucci syndrome develop multiple enchondromas and spindle cell hemangiomas and are also at risk of developing other malignancies, including brain gliomas, another type of cancer associated with IDH gene mutations (Chapter 28). Chondrosarcoma Chondrosarcomas are malignant tumors that produce cartilage. After osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma is the second most common malignant matrix-producing tumor of bone. These tumors are subclassified into hyaline cartilage-producing (conventional), clear cell, dedifferentiated, and mesenchymal subtypes. Conventional chondrosarcomas represent approximately 90% of all chondrosarcomas and arise in individuals in their fourth decade or older. Men are affected twice as frequently as women. Conventional chondrosarcomas commonly arise in the axial skeleton, especially the pelvis, shoulder, and ribs, but unlike benign enchondroma, distal extremities are rarely involved. About 15% of conventional chondrosarcomas are secondary and arise from preexisting enchondromas or osteochondromas. On imaging, the calcified matrix of chondrosarcomas appears as foci of flocculent densities. Slow-growing low-grade tumors cause reactive cortical thickening, whereas aggressive high-grade neoplasms destroy the cortex and form soft tissue masses (Fig. 26.23A).

The clear cell and mesenchymal variants occur in younger people in their teens or 20s. The clear cell variant is unique in that it originates in the epiphyses of long tubular bones.

Pathogenesis

Although chondrosarcomas are genetically heterogeneous, a few recurrent driver mutations are recognized. Chondrosarcomas arising in multiple osteochondroma syndrome exhibit mutations in the EXT1 or EXT2 genes that regulate the synthesis of cartilaginous matrix proteins. Both chondromatosis-related and sporadic chondrosarcomas may have IDH1 or IDH2 mutations. Silencing of the CDKN2A tumor suppressor locus by DNA methylation is common in sporadic tumors.

MORPHOLOGY
Conventional chondrosarcomas are bulky tumors made up of nodules of
glistening gray-white, translucent cartilage, but the matrix is often gelatinous or myxoid and can ooze from the cut surface (Fig. 26.23B). Focal calcifications may be present and central necrosis may create cystic spaces.
Extracortical extension into surrounding muscle and fat is common.
Histologically, the cartilage infiltrates the marrow space and surrounds
preexisting bony trabeculae (Fig. 26.23C). Chondrosarcomas vary in cellularity, degree of cytologic atypia, and mitotic activity and on this basis are
assigned a grade from 1 to 3 that correlates well with prognosis. Grade 1
tumors have low cellularity and contain neoplastic chondrocytes with plump
vesicular nuclei and small nucleoli. By contrast, grade 3 chondrosarcomas
show high cellularity, extreme pleomorphism and frequent mitotic figures
(Fig. 26.23D).
Dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma consists of a low-grade chondrosarcoma with a second, high-grade component that does not produce cartilage.
Clear-cell chondrosarcoma contains sheets of large, atypical chondrocytes
that have abundant clear cytoplasm, numerous osteoclast-type giant cells, and
intralesional bone formation. Mesenchymal chondrosarcoma is composed
of islands of well-differentiated hyaline cartilage surrounded by sheets of
primitive appearing small round cells.
Clinical Features
Chondrosarcomas typically present as painful, progressively enlarging
masses. The histologic grade and anatomic site correlate with biologic
behavior. Grade 1 tumors rarely metastasize, locally recur in approximately 10% of cases, and have 5-year survival rates of close to 100%.
Mortality derives from local recurrence, which is most problematic in
the limb girdles and axial skeleton. Accordingly, grade 1 tumors in the
long bones of the extremities have a good prognosis. Consequently, the
diagnosis atypical cartilaginous tumor has been proposed for grade 1
chondrosarcomas of the extremities. By contrast, most grade 3 tumors
spread hematogenously, especially to the lungs, and 5-year survival is
less than 50%. Treatment ranges from curettage in select cases of grade

Aneurysmal Bone Cyst
Aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign neoplasm characterized by
multiloculated blood-filled spaces . All age groups are affected, but
most cases present in adolescence. ABC develops most frequently in
the femur, tibia, and vertebral body posterior elements (lamina and
pedicles).
Pathogenesis
The spindle-shaped tumor cells of ABC are of uncertain origin and demonstrate
rearrangements of chromosome 17p13 that result in fusion of
the coding region of the USP6 gene with the regulatory regions of numerous
other genes, most commonly CDH11 , leading to overexpression
of USP6 protein. USP6 is a deubiquitinating enzyme that enhances the
activity of the transcription factor NF-κB. This in turn up-regulates expression
of proteins such as matrix metalloproteases, leading to cystic

periosteum, and soft tissue. Grossly, the tumor is soft, tan-white, and frequently contains areas of hemorrhage and necrosis. Microscopically, it is

lymphocytes (Fig. 26.24). They have scant cytoplasm that may be clear because
of the presence of glycogen. Homer-Wright rosettes, circular groups of cells
with a central fibrillary core, may be present. Fibrous septa may be seen, but
the tumor cells do not produce bone or cartilage.

Although Ewing sarcoma is aggressive, neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgical excision and adjuvant chemotherapy, with or without
radiation, has achieved 75% 5-year survival and 50% long-term cure
