Giant Cell Tumor
Giant cell tumor is a neoplasm composed of monotonous mononuclear stromal cells, macrophages, and osteoclast-type giant cells.
This uncommon tumor usually arises in the third through fifth decades of life, typically in the epiphyses of long bones. While benign,
they can be locally aggressive.
Pathogenesis
Most of the cells within giant cell tumors are nonneoplastic osteoclasts
and their precursors. The neoplastic cells are primitive osteoblast precursors that express high levels of RANKL, which promotes the proliferation of osteoclast precursors and their differentiation into mature
osteoclasts. The absence of normal feedback between osteoblasts and
osteoclasts results in localized, but highly destructive, bone resorption.
The neoplastic cells have acquired mutations in the H3-3A gene encoding histone 3.3, a chromatin packaging protein; precisely how this
leads to tumor formation is unknown.
Giant cell tumors develop within the epiphysis and may extend
into the metaphysis. The majority occur near the knee in the distal
femur or proximal tibia, but virtually any bone can be involved.
Because they typically arise near joints, giant cell tumors may cause
arthritis-like symptoms. They may also present with pathologic
fractures.

Giant cell tumors often destroy the overlying cortex, resulting in a bulging
soft tissue mass delineated by a thin shell of reactive bone (Fig. 26.25A).

cystic degeneration. Histologically, the tumors consist of uniform oval
mononuclear tumor cells and abundant osteoclast-type giant cells with
100 or more nuclei (Fig. 26.25B). Necrosis and mitotic activity may be
prominent.

Giant cell tumors are treated by curettage, but 40% to 60% recur
locally. Although up to 4% metastasize to the lungs, these regress spontaneously or can be cured by excision. The RANKL inhibitor denosumab has shown promise as an alternative to surgery in cases in
which resection would lead to significant morbidity.

rates. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy–induced necrosis is a positive prognostic indicator. Giant Cell Tumor Giant cell tumor is a neoplasm composed of monotonous mononuclear stromal cells, macrophages, and osteoclast-type giant cells. This uncommon tumor usually arises in the third through fifth decades of life, typically in the epiphyses of long bones. While benign, they can be locally aggressive.
Pathogenesis

Most of the cells within giant cell tumors are nonneoplastic osteoclasts and their precursors. The neoplastic cells are primitive osteoblast precursors that express high levels of RANKL, which promotes the proliferation of osteoclast precursors and their differentiation into mature osteoclasts. The absence of normal feedback between osteoblasts and osteoclasts results in localized, but highly destructive, bone resorption. The neoplastic cells have acquired mutations in the H3-3A gene encoding histone 3.3, a chromatin packaging protein; precisely how this leads to tumor formation is unknown.

Giant cell tumors develop within the epiphysis and may extend into the metaphysis. The majority occur near the knee in the distal femur or proximal tibia, but virtually any bone can be involved. Because they typically arise near joints, giant cell tumors may cause arthritis-like symptoms. They may also present with pathologic fractures.
MORPHOLOGY

Giant cell tumors often destroy the overlying cortex, resulting in a bulging soft tissue mass delineated by a thin shell of reactive bone (Fig. 26.25A). Grossly, the tumors are large, red-brown masses that frequently undergo cystic degeneration. Histologically, the tumors consist of uniform oval mononuclear tumor cells and abundant osteoclast-type giant cells with 100 or more nuclei (Fig. 26.25B). Necrosis and mitotic activity may be prominent.
Clinical Features

Giant cell tumors are treated by curettage, but 40% to 60% recur locally. Although up to 4% metastasize to the lungs, these regress spontaneously or can be cured by excision. The RANKL inhibitor denosumab has shown promise as an alternative to surgery in cases in which resection would lead to significant morbidity.
Aneurysmal Bone Cyst

Aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign neoplasm characterized by multiloculated blood-filled spaces. All age groups are affected, but most cases present in adolescence. ABC develops most frequently in the femur, tibia, and vertebral body posterior elements (lamina and pedicles).
Pathogenesis

The spindle-shaped tumor cells of ABC are of uncertain origin and demonstrate rearrangements of chromosome 17p13 that result in fusion of the coding region of the USP6 gene with the regulatory regions of numerous other genes, most commonly CDH11, leading to overexpression of USP6 protein. USP6 is a deubiquitinating enzyme that enhances the activity of the transcription factor NF-κB. This in turn up-regulates expression of proteins such as matrix metalloproteases, leading to cystic bone resorption.

Fig. 26.25 Giant cell tumor of bone. (A) Giant cell tumor of the proximal fibula is predominantly lytic and
expansile with destruction of the cortex. A pathologic fracture is also present. (B) Giant cell tumor illustrating
an abundance of osteoclast-type multinucleated giant cells with background mononuclear stromal cells.
MORPHOLOGY
Radiographically, ABC is usually an eccentric, expansile, well-circumscribed
lytic lesion with well-defined margins. Most show central lysis and a thin sclerotic “eggshell” of reactive bone at the periphery. Computed tomography and
magnetic resonance imaging may demonstrate internal septa and c haracteristic
fluid-fluid levels (Fig. 26.26A). Grossly, ABCs consist of multiple blood-filled
cystic spaces separated by thin, tan-white septa (Fig. 26.26B). Microscopically,
the septa are composed of plump spindle cells, multinucleated osteoclast-like
giant cells, and reactive woven bone lined by osteoblasts (Fig. 26.27). The septa
lack an endothelial lining and so are not true aneurysms. Bone deposition typically follows the contours of fibrous septa. Approximately one-third of cases
contain an unusual densely calcified, basophilic metaplastic matrix referred to
as blue bone. Necrosis is uncommon unless a pathologic fracture is present.
Clinical Features
ABC presents with localized pain and swelling. Vertebral lesions may
produce nerve compression. Despite being benign, ABC is locally aggressive. Treatment is by curettage or excision. Recurrence occurs in
10% to 50% of cases.
Nonossifying Fibroma
Nonossifying fibroma is a benign spindle cell tumor with osteoclast-type giant cells. These lesions are present in up to 50% of children older than 2 years of age and typically present as an incidental
finding in adolescents. The vast majority arise eccentrically in the
metaphysis of the distal femur and proximal tibia. Multifocal nonossifying fibromas may occur in the setting of neurofibromatosis type 1
(NF1) and Jaffe-Campanacci syndrome, which may represent a subtype
of NF1. Most are less than 0.5 cm in diameter, but they occasionally
may grow to 5 cm or larger in size.
Pathogenesis
Activating mutations in KRAS and FGFR1 genes have been identified
in sporadic tumors, whereas mutations in NF1 are present in NF1 and
Jaffe-Campanacci patients with nonossifying fibromas. These findings
indicate that nonossifying fibromas are true neoplasms, albeit
with limited growth potential, that are driven by activation of the RAS
pathway.
MORPHOLOGY
Nonossifying fibromas are sharply demarcated radiolucent masses surrounded
by a thin rim of sclerosis (Fig. 26.28A). Grossly, they are grey to yellow-brown
and lack mineralization. Microscopically, they consist of bland fibroblasts that
are frequently arranged in a storiform (pinwheel) pattern and macrophages
that can take the form of clustered cells with foamy cytoplasm or multinucleated giant cells (Fig. 26.28B). Hemosiderin is commonly present.
Clinical Features
Nonossifying fibromas are asymptomatic and are detected incidentally
on radiographic studies. The radiographic findings are sufficiently
specific that biopsy is rarely necessary. Most small lesions have limited
growth potential and undergo spontaneous resolution over several
years as they are replaced by normal cortical bone. The few that progressively enlarge may present with pathologic fracture and require
biopsy to exclude other types of tumors. They are treated with curettage and may require bone grafting.
Fibrous Dysplasia
Fibrous dysplasia is a benign neoplasm of bone characterized by
disorganized and inadequately mineralized bone and intervening
fibrous tissue. The lesions arise during skeletal development and may
be sporadic or syndromic. They present in several ways, as follows:
• Monostotic: involvement of a single bone
• Polyostotic: involvement of multiple bones
• Mazabraud syndrome: fibrous dysplasia and soft tissue myxomas
• McCune-Albright syndrome: polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, café-
au-lait skin pigmentations, and endocrine abnormalities, especially precocious puberty
Pathogenesis
All forms of fibrous dysplasia result from somatic gain-of-function
mutations in the gene GNAS1 during fetal development. GNAS1
encodes the stimulatory a subunit of the GTP-binding protein Gs
and is also mutated in pituitary neuroendocrine tumors (Chapter 24).
The mutations produce constitutive activation of Gs, which leads to
increased intracellular levels of the signaling molecule cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP). This in turn alters the activity of

Nonossifying fibromas are sharply demarcated radiolucent masses surrounded by a thin rim of sclerosis (Fig. 26.28A). Grossly, they are grey to yellow-brown and lack mineralization. Microscopically, they consist of bland fibroblasts that are frequently arranged in a storiform (pinwheel) pattern and macrophages that can take the form of clustered cells with foamy cytoplasm or multinucleated giant cells (Fig. 26.28B). Hemosiderin is commonly present. Clinical Features Nonossifying fibromas are asymptomatic and are detected incidentally on radiographic studies. The radiographic findings are sufficiently specific that biopsy is rarely necessary. Most small lesions have limited growth potential and undergo spontaneous resolution over several years as they are replaced by normal cortical bone. The few that progressively enlarge may present with pathologic fracture and require biopsy to exclude other types of tumors. They are treated with curettage and may require bone grafting. Fibrous Dysplasia Fibrous dysplasia is a benign neoplasm of bone characterized by disorganized and inadequately mineralized bone and intervening fibrous tissue. The lesions arise during skeletal development and may be sporadic or syndromic. They present in several ways, as follows:

• Monostotic: involvement of a single bone

• Polyostotic: involvement of multiple bones

• Mazabraud syndrome: fibrous dysplasia and soft tissue myxomas

• McCune-Albright syndrome: polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, café- au-lait skin pigmentations, and endocrine abnormalities, especially precocious puberty Pathogenesis All forms of fibrous dysplasia result from somatic gain-of-function mutations in the gene GNAS1 during fetal development. GNAS1 encodes the stimulatory a subunit of the GTP-binding protein Gs and is also mutated in pituitary neuroendocrine tumors (Chapter 24). The mutations produce constitutive activation of Gs, which leads to increased intracellular levels of the signaling molecule cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP). The most common clinical presentation of McCune-Albright syndrome is precocious sexual development, primarily in girls. The syndrome can include other endocrinopathies such as hyperthyroidism,
pituitary neuroendocrine tumors that secrete growth hormone, and
primary adrenal hyperplasia (see Chapter 24). Bone lesions are often
unilateral and skin lesions, when present, are limited to the same side
of the body. Skeletal manifestations are managed as for polyostotic
fibrous dysplasia, while the endocrinopathies are treated medically
(e.g., with aromatase inhibitors for precocious puberty).
Metastatic Tumors
Cancers of extraosseous origin are the most common form of malignancy to involve the skeleton, greatly outnumbering primary
bone cancers. The pathways of spread to bone include (1) direct extension, (2) lymphatic or hematogenous dissemination, and (3) intraspinal seeding (via the Batson plexus of veins). Any cancer can
spread to bone, but in adults more than 75% of skeletal metastases
originate from carcinomas of the prostate, breast, kidney, and lung.
In children, neuroblastoma, Wilms tumor, osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma most commonly produce metastases
to bone. Skeletal metastases are typically multifocal and tend to
involve the axial skeleton, especially the vertebral column. However, carcinomas of the kidney and thyroid may present as solitary
skeletal metastases.
The radiographic appearance of metastases may be purely lytic
(bone destroying), purely blastic (bone forming), or mixed (lytic
and blastic). Some carcinomas, for example prostatic adenocarcinoma, produce predominantly blastic metastases, whereas kidney
and breast carcinomas produce lytic lesions. Bidirectional interactions between metastatic cancer cells and native bone cells account
for these varied features. Tumor cells do not directly resorb bone
in lytic lesions, but they secrete substances such as prostaglandins,
cytokines, and PTH-related peptide that stimulate osteoclast activity. Conversely, as bone is resorbed, matrix-bound growth factors
(e.g., TGF-β, IGF-1, and FGF) are released that support the growth
of metastatic tumor cells. Blastic metastases may result from tumor cells secreting Wnt proteins that stimulate osteoblastic bone
formation.
The presence of bone metastases generally portends a poor prognosis because it indicates wide disease dissemination, but metastatic
breast and prostate cancers can sometimes be managed for many years
with hormone therapy. For other cancers, treatment options include
systemic chemotherapy or immunotherapy, localized radiation, and
bisphosphonates. Surgery may be necessary to stabilize pathologic
fractures.

unilateral and skin lesions, when present, are limited to the same side

Metastatic Tumors
Cancers of extraosseous origin are the most common form of ma-
lignancy to involve the skeleton, greatly outnumbering primary
bone cancers. The pathways of spread to bone include (1) direct ex-
tension, (2) lymphatic or hematogenous dissemination, and (3) in-
traspinal seeding (via the Batson plexus of veins). Any cancer can
spread to bone, but in adults more than 75% of skeletal metastases
originate from carcinomas of the prostate, breast, kidney, and lung.
In children, neuroblastoma, Wilms tumor, osteosarcoma, Ewing sar-
coma, and rhabdomyosarcoma most commonly produce metastases
to bone. Skeletal metastases are typically multifocal and tend to
involve the axial skeleton, especially the vertebral column. How-
ever, carcinomas of the kidney and thyroid may present as solitary
skeletal metastases.
The radiographic appearance of metastases may be purely lytic

and blastic). Some carcinomas, for example prostatic adenocarci-

cytokines, and PTH-related peptide that stimulate osteoclast activ-

formation.

sis because it indicates wide disease dissemination, but metastatic
breast and prostate cancers can sometimes be managed for many years
with hormone therapy. For other cancers, treatment options include
systemic chemotherapy or immunotherapy, localized radiation, and
bisphosphonates. Surgery may be necessary to stabilize pathologic
fractures.

1088 CHAPTER 26 Bones, Joints, and Soft Tissue Tumors
KEY CONCEPTS
Bone Tumors
Most bone tumors are classified according to the normal cell they resemble or
the matrix they produce; the remainder are grouped by clinicopathologic features. Most primary bone tumors are benign. Metastases, especially adenocarcinomas, are more common than primary bone neoplasms.
Major categories of primary bone tumors include:
• Bone forming: Osteoblastoma and osteoid osteoma consist of benign
osteoblasts that synthesize osteoid. Osteosarcoma is a tumor of malignant
osteoblasts with an aggressive clinical course that predominantly involves
adolescents.
• Cartilage forming: Osteochondroma is an exostosis with a cartilage cap.
Syndromic forms are most often associated with germline mutations in EXT
genes. Chondromas are benign intramedullary tumors that produce hyaline
cartilage and usually arise in the digits. Chondrosarcomas are malignant
tumors of cartilage involving the axial skeleton in adults.
• Ewing sarcoma is an aggressive malignant small round cell tumor most
often associated with fusion of the EWSR1 and FLI1 genes.
• Nonossifying fibroma and fibrous dysplasia are benign osseous neoplasms
driven by activation of the RAS pathway and gain-of-function mutations in
the GNAS1 gene, respectively.
JOINTS
Joints allow movement while providing mechanical stability. They
are classified as solid (nonsynovial) and cavitated (synovial). The
solid joints, or synarthroses, provide structural integrity, lack a joint
space, and allow only minimal movement. They are grouped according to the type of connective tissue (fibrous tissue or cartilage) that
bridges the ends of the bones. Fibrous synarthroses include the
cranial sutures and the bonds between roots of teeth and the jawbones. Cartilage synarthroses include the sternocostal joints and
pubic symphysis. Synovial joints, by contrast, have a joint space that
allows a wide range of motion. Synovial membranes enclose the
joints and are firmly anchored to an overlying fibrous capsule reinforced by ligaments and muscle. Synovial membranes are lined by
two types of cells arranged in layers. Type A synoviocytes are specialized macrophages with phagocytic a ctivity. Type B synoviocytes are
similar to fibroblasts and synthesize hyaluronic acid and various
proteins. The synovial lining lacks a basement membrane, which
allows for efficient exchange of nutrients, waste, and gases between
blood and synovial fluid, a hyaluronic acid–rich plasma filtrate that
acts as a viscous lubricant and provides nutrition for the articular
cartilage.
Hyaline cartilage is a unique connective tissue ideally suited to
serve as an elastic shock absorber and wear-resistant surface. It is
composed of water (70%), type II collagen (10%), proteoglycans (8%),
and chondrocytes. The collagen fibers enable resistance to tensile
stresses and transmit vertical loads; water and proteoglycans limit
compression and friction. Hyaline cartilage lacks blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerves. Chondrocytes synthesize the matrix and secrete
enzymes that remodel it. The activity of these enzymes is held in
check by inhibitors that are also secreted by chondrocytes. Diseases
that destroy articular cartilage alter this balance by increasing the
activity of degradative enzymes and decreasing the production of
their inhibitors. Among the factors implicated in triggering the degradative process are cytokines such as IL-1 and TNF, which may be
released by inflammatory cells and chondrocytes, synoviocytes, fibroblasts, and inflammatory cells.
ARTHRITIS
Arthritis is inflammation of joints. The most important forms of
arthritis are osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, which differ in
pathogenesis and clinical and pathologic manifestations (discussed
later). Other types of arthritis are caused by immune reactions, infections, and crystal deposition.
Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis (OA), also called degenerative joint disease, is characterized by cartilage degeneration that results in structural and
functional failure of synovial joints. It is the most common type of
joint disease. Although the term osteoarthritis implies an inflammatory disease, it is primarily a degenerative disease of articular cartilage,
with inflammation acting as a secondary contributor.
In most instances, OA appears insidiously, without apparent initiating cause, as an aging phenomenon (idiopathic or primary osteoarthritis). In these cases, the disease usually affects few joints (oligoarticular)
but may be generalized. In about 5% of cases, OA appears in younger
individuals with predisposing conditions, such as a joint deformity, a
previous joint injury, or an underlying systemic disease (diabetes, obesity, ochronosis) that places joints at risk. In these settings, the disease
is called secondary osteoarthritis. The association with aging is strong;
the prevalence of OA increases exponentially beyond 50 years of age,
and about 40% of people older than 70 years are affected.
Pathogenesis
The lesions of OA stem from degeneration of articular cartilage and
disordered repair. Biomechanical stress is the principal pathogenic
mechanism, but genetic factors, including polymorphisms in genes encoding components of the matrix and signaling molecules, may predispose to chondrocyte injury that causes matrix alteration (Fig. 26.30). In
the early stages of OA, chondrocytes proliferate (likely in response to
matrix loss) and continue to synthesize proteoglycans, but degradation
exceeds synthesis. Concurrently, the water content of the matrix increases. Chondrocytes also secrete MMPs that degrade the type II collagen network. The normal horizontally arranged collagen fibers are
cleaved, producing fissures and clefts at the articular surface. Cytokines
and diffusible factors from chondrocytes and synovial cells, particularly
TGF-β (which induces the production of MMPs), IL-1, IL-6, prostaglandins, and nitric oxide, are also implicated in OA, and chronic low-level
inflammation contributes to disease progression. Bone morphogenetic
proteins and TGF-β appear to play a central role in the development of
osteophytes, bony outgrowths at the periphery of the articular surface.
MORPHOLOGY
In early OA, chondrocytes proliferate and form clusters. As type II collagen and
proteoglycans are degraded, the resulting fissures and clefts create a granular
and soft articular surface (Fig. 26.31A). In advanced OA, sloughed full-thickness
portions of cartilage tumble into the joint, forming loose bodies (joint mice).
The exposed subchondral bone becomes the new articular surface, which is
burnished by friction with the opposing surface, giving it the appearance of
polished ivory (bone eburnation) (Fig. 26.31B). Small fractures develop in the
subarticular bone, creating gaps that allow synovial fluid to be forced into the
subchondral regions in a ball valve-like mechanism, leading to fibrous-walled
cysts. Mushroom-shaped bony outgrowths (osteophytes) develop at the margins of the articular surface and are capped by fibrocartilage and hyaline cartilage that gradually ossify. Advanced OA manifests radiographically as loss of
joint space, subchondral sclerotic bone, and osteophytes (Fig. 26.32), findings
that are sufficiently diagnostic that biopsy is not required. The synovium is usually only mildly congested and fibrotic and contains few inflammatory cells.

1088 CHAPTER ₂₆ Bones, Joints, and Soft Tissue Tumors
KEY CONCEPTS
Bone Tumors
Most bone tumors are classified according to the normal cell they resemble or
the matrix they produce; the remainder are grouped by clinicopathologic fea-
tures. Most primary bone tumors are benign. Metastases, especially adenocar-
cinomas, are more common than primary bone neoplasms.
Major categories of primary bone tumors include:
• Bone forming: Osteoblastoma and osteoid osteoma consist of benign
osteoblasts that synthesize osteoid. Osteosarcoma is a tumor of malignant
osteoblasts with an aggressive clinical course that predominantly involves
adolescents.
• Cartilage forming: Osteochondroma is an exostosis with a cartilage cap.
Syndromic forms are most often associated with germline mutations in EXT
genes. Chondromas are benign intramedullary tumors that produce hyaline
cartilage and usually arise in the digits. Chondrosarcomas are malignant
tumors of cartilage involving the axial skeleton in adults.
• Ewing sarcoma is an aggressive malignant small round cell tumor most
often associated with fusion of the EWSR1 and FLI1 genes.
• Nonossifying fibroma and fibrous dysplasia are benign osseous neoplasms
driven by activation of the RAS pathway and gain-of-function mutations in
the GNAS1 gene, respectively.
JOINTS
Joints allow movement while providing mechanical stability. They
are classified as solid (nonsynovial) and cavitated (synovial). The
solid joints, or synarthroses, provide structural integrity, lack a joint
space, and allow only minimal movement. They are grouped accord-
ing to the type of connective tissue (fibrous tissue or cartilage) that
bridges the ends of the bones. Fibrous synarthroses include the
cranial sutures and the bonds between roots of teeth and the jaw-
bones. Cartilage synarthroses include the sternocostal joints and
pubic symphysis. Synovial joints, by contrast, have a joint space that
allows a wide range of motion. Synovial membranes enclose the
joints and are firmly anchored to an overlying fibrous capsule rein-
forced by ligaments and muscle. Synovial membranes are lined by
two types of cells arranged in layers. Type A synoviocytes are special-
ized macrophages with phagocytic a ctivity. Type B synoviocytes are
similar to fibroblasts and synthesize hyaluronic acid and various
proteins. The synovial lining lacks a basement membrane, which
allows for efficient exchange of nutrients, waste, and gases between
blood and synovial fluid, a hyaluronic acid–rich plasma filtrate that
acts as a viscous lubricant and provides nutrition for the articular
cartilage.
Hyaline cartilage is a unique connective tissue ideally suited to
serve as an elastic shock absorber and wear-resistant surface. It is
composed of water (70%), type II collagen (10%), proteoglycans (8%),
and chondrocytes. The collagen fibers enable resistance to tensile
stresses and transmit vertical loads; water and proteoglycans limit
compression and friction. Hyaline cartilage lacks blood vessels, lym-
phatics, and nerves. Chondrocytes synthesize the matrix and secrete
enzymes that remodel it. The activity of these enzymes is held in
check by inhibitors that are also secreted by chondrocytes. Diseases
that destroy articular cartilage alter this balance by increasing the
activity of degradative enzymes and decreasing the production of
their inhibitors. Among the factors implicated in triggering the deg-
radative process are cytokines such as IL-1 and TNF, which may be
released by inflammatory cells and chondrocytes, synoviocytes, fibro-
blasts, and inflammatory cells.
ARTHRITIS
Arthritis is inflammation of joints. The most important forms of
arthritis are osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, which differ in
pathogenesis and clinical and pathologic manifestations (discussed
later). Other types of arthritis are caused by immune reactions, infec-
tions, and crystal deposition.
Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis (OA), also called degenerative joint disease, is char-
acterized by cartilage degeneration that results in structural and
functional failure of synovial joints. It is the most common type of
joint disease. Although the term osteoarthritis implies an inflamma-
tory disease, it is primarily a degenerative disease of articular cartilage,
with inflammation acting as a secondary contributor.
In most instances, OA appears insidiously, without apparent initiat-
ing cause, as an aging phenomenon (idiopathic or primary osteoarthri-
tis). In these cases, the disease usually affects few joints (oligoarticular)
but may be generalized. In about 5% of cases, OA appears in younger
individuals with predisposing conditions, such as a joint deformity, a
previous joint injury, or an underlying systemic disease (diabetes, obe-
sity, ochronosis) that places joints at risk. In these settings, the disease
is called secondary osteoarthritis. The association with aging is strong;
the prevalence of OA increases exponentially beyond 50 years of age,
and about 40% of people older than 70 years are affected.
Pathogenesis
The lesions of OA stem from degeneration of articular cartilage and
disordered repair. Biomechanical stress is the principal pathogenic
mechanism, but genetic factors, including polymorphisms in genes en-
coding components of the matrix and signaling molecules, may predis-
pose to chondrocyte injury that causes matrix alteration (Fig. 26.30). In
the early stages of OA, chondrocytes proliferate (likely in response to
matrix loss) and continue to synthesize proteoglycans, but degradation
exceeds synthesis. Concurrently, the water content of the matrix in-
creases. Chondrocytes also secrete MMPs that degrade the type II col-
lagen network. The normal horizontally arranged collagen fibers are
cleaved, producing fissures and clefts at the articular surface. Cytokines
and diffusible factors from chondrocytes and synovial cells, particularly
TGF-b (which induces the production of MMPs), IL-1, IL-6, prostaglan-
dins, and nitric oxide, are also implicated in OA, and chronic low-level
inflammation contributes to disease progression. Bone morphogenetic
proteins and TGF-b appear to play a central role in the development of
osteophytes, bony outgrowths at the periphery of the articular surface.
MORPHOLOGY
In early OA, chondrocytes proliferate and form clusters. As type II collagen and
proteoglycans are degraded, the resulting fissures and clefts create a granular
and soft articular surface (Fig. 26.31A). In advanced OA, sloughed full-thickness
portions of cartilage tumble into the joint, forming loose bodies (joint mice).
The exposed subchondral bone becomes the new articular surface, which is
burnished by friction with the opposing surface, giving it the appearance of
polished ivory (bone eburnation) (Fig. 26.31B). Small fractures develop in the
subarticular bone, creating gaps that allow synovial fluid to be forced into the
subchondral regions in a ball valve-like mechanism, leading to fibrous-walled
cysts. Mushroom-shaped bony outgrowths (osteophytes) develop at the mar-
gins of the articular surface and are capped by fibrocartilage and hyaline carti-
lage that gradually ossify. Advanced OA manifests radiographically as loss of
joint space, subchondral sclerotic bone, and osteophytes (Fig. 26.32), findings
that are sufficiently diagnostic that biopsy is not required. The synovium is usu-
ally only mildly congested and fibrotic and contains few inflammatory cells.

RA typically manifests as a symmetric arthritis of the small joints of the hands
and feet. The synovium becomes edematous, thickened, and hyperplastic,
transforming its smooth contour to one covered by delicate and bulbous villi
(Fig. 26.34). The characteristic histologic features include (1) synovial cell hyperplasia and proliferation; (2) dense inflammatory infiltrates of CD4⁺
helper T cells, B cells (frequently forming lymphoid follicles), plasma cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages; (3) increased vascularity due to angiogenesis; (4)
fibrin-rich exudate containing neutrophils on the synovial and joint surfaces; and
(5) osteoclastic activity in subchondral bone, allowing the inflamed synovium to
penetrate the bone and cause periarticular erosions and subchondral cysts. Together, these changes produce the pannus, a mass of edematous synovium,
inflammatory cells, granulation tissue, and fibroblasts that grows over and
causes erosion of articular cartilage. In time, after the cartilage has been destroyed, the pannus bridges the apposing bones to form a fibrous ankylosis,
which eventually ossifies and results in bone fusion, or bony ankyloses.
Rheumatoid nodules are an infrequent manifestation of RA and typically
occur in the subcutaneous tissue of the forearm, elbows, occiput, and lumbosacral area. These are small, firm, nontender, oval masses. Microscopically,
they have a central zone of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by a prominent rim of
activated macrophages and numerous lymphocytes and plasma cells
(Fig. 26.35). Severe disease may be associated with leukocytoclastic vasculitis (Chapter 11), an acute necrotizing vasculitis of small and large arteries
that may involve pleura, pericardium, or lung and evolve into a chronic fibrosing process. Ocular changes such as uveitis and keratoconjunctivitis (similar to
Sjögren syndrome, Chapter 6) may also occur.

before larger ones. Symptoms usually develop in the hands and feet,
followed in decreasing frequency by the wrists, ankles, elbows, and
knees. In the hands, the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints are involved, in contrast to OA (see earlier). While
laboratory tests for ACPA and rheumatoid factor aid in diagnosis,
about 20% of patients with RA are seronegative; in these cases, diagnosis is based on the clinical and radiographic findings. Tissue biopsy is rarely necessary.
Involved joints are swollen, warm, and painful. Unlike OA, pain is
usually worse in the morning or following inactivity. Typically, RA
pursues a chronic, waxing and waning course that leads to progressive
joint enlargement and decreasing range of motion. In a minority of
individuals, especially those lacking ACPA and rheumatoid factor, the

Reactive Arthritis
Reactive arthritis is defined by the triad of arthritis, nongonococcal
urethritis or cervicitis, and conjunctivitis following an infection.
More recently, the definition has been broadened to include mono- or
oligoarticular arthritis that occurs days to weeks after genitourinary
(Chlamydia) or gastrointestinal (Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia, Campylobacter, and Clostridioides difficile) infections. HIV-positive patients
may also be affected; the reactive arthritis in these individuals is
thought to be caused by pathogens other than HIV. HLA-B27 is common in patients with reactive arthritis. The disease most often presents
in young adults, with a global prevalence of approximately 30 per
100,000 adults. Arthritic episodes usually wax and wane over a period
of months, but nearly 50% of patients have recurrent arthritis, tendon-itis, and lumbosacral pain. Spondyloarthritis can occur in these
patients, and spine involvement can be indistinguishable from ankylosing spondylitis.

Mycobacterial Arthritis
Mycobacterial arthritis is a chronic progressive joint disorder
caused by M. tuberculosis infection. It occurs primarily in adults
as a complication of adjacent osteomyelitis or after hematogenous
dissemination from a visceral (usually pulmonary) site of infection.
Onset is insidious and associated with gradually increasing
pain. Mycobacterial seeding of the joint induces formation of confluent
caseating granulomas. The synovium may grow as a pannus
over the articular cartilage and erode the bone along the joint
margins. Chronic disease results in fibrous ankylosis and obliteration
of the joint space. Weight-bearing joints, especially the hips,
knees, and ankles, in descending order of frequency, are most
commonly affected.
Viral Arthritis
Arthritis can occur with a variety of viral infections. The most common
are alphavirus, parvovirus B19, rubella, Epstein-Barr virus, and
hepatitis B and C viruses. The manifestations range from acute to
subacute arthritis. Joint symptoms may be caused by direct infection of
the joint by the virus, as in rubella and some alphavirus infections, or
by an autoimmune reaction triggered by the infection.

triggering inflammatory reactions that destroy cartilage.
Gout
Gout is marked by transient attacks of acute arthritis initiated by
monosodium urate crystals deposited within and around joints.

disease (Table 26.6), the common feature is excessive uric acid in the
tissues and body fluids. In the primary form (90% of cases), gout is the
major manifestation of the disease.

acid levels are determined by several factors:

lism. Increased synthesis typically reflects some abnormality in

pathways: the de novo pathway, in which purine nucleotides
are  synthesized  from  nonpurine  precursors,  and  the  salvage
pathway,  in  which  nucleotides  are  synthesized  from  free

ron and excreted in the urine.
In primary gout, elevated uric acid most commonly results from
reduced excretion, the basis of which is unknown in most patients.
Genome-wide association studies have identified polymorphisms in
genes including URAT1, GLUT9, and KCNQ1, which are involved in
transport and homeostasis of urate and other ions. In a small minority
of cases primary gout is caused by increased uric acid production due
to enzymatic defects. For example, partial deficiency of hypoxanthine
guanine phosphoribosyl transferase (HGPRT) interrupts the salvage
pathway, so purine metabolites cannot be recycled and are instead
degraded into uric acid. Complete absence of HGPRT also results in
hyperuricemia, but a significant neurologic condition (Lesch-Nyhan
syndrome) dominates the clinical picture, so this is considered a form

medications or conditions that cause hyperuricemia. Secondary gout
can also be caused by increased synthesis of uric acid (e.g., following
rapid cell lysis during chemotherapy for leukemia) or decreased excre-
tion (chronic renal disease).
The arthritis in gout is triggered by precipitation of monoso-
dium urate crystals into the joints, which results in the production
of cytokines that recruit leukocytes (Fig. 26.38). Resident synovial
macrophages and neutrophils phagocytose the urate crystals, which
are detected by a cytosolic sensor, the inflammasome (Chapter 3). In
response, the inflammasome activates caspase-1, which is involved in
the production of active IL-1. IL-1 promotes accumulation of more
neutrophils and macrophages within the joint. Ingested urate crystals
may also rupture phagolysosomes, releasing additional proteases and
inflammatory mediators. A vicious cycle develops as newly recruited
inflammatory cells release cytokines, free radicals, proteases, and ara-
chidonic acid metabolites to recruit even more leukocytes. Comple-
ment activation by the alternative pathway may further contribute to
leukocyte recruitment. The result is an acute arthritis that typically
remits in days to weeks. However, repeated attacks of acute arthritis
lead eventually to the formation of tophi, aggregates of urate crystals
and inflammatory tissue in the inflamed synovial membrane and peri-
articular tissue, as well as severe cartilage damage that compromises
joint function.
Only about 10% of individuals with hyperuricemia develop gout.
Other factors linked to disease include:
•  Age of the individual and duration of the hyperuricemia. Gout usu-
ally appears after 20 to 30 years of hyperuricemia
•  Genetic predisposition. In addition to X-linked HGPRT abnormali-
ties, polymorphisms in genes involved with urate or ion transport
and inflammation are associated with gout
•  Alcohol consumption
•  Obesity
•  Drugs (e.g., thiazides) that reduce urate excretion

tains scattered lymphocytes, plasma cells, and macrophages. The acute attack
remits when the episode of crystallization abates and crystals are solubilized.
Chronic tophaceous arthritis evolves from repetitive precipitation of urate
crystals during acute attacks. Urate crystals encrust the articular surface and form

Resident synovial macrophages and neutrophils phagocytose the urate crystals, which are detected by a cytosolic sensor, the inflammasome (Chapter 3). In response, the inflammasome activates caspase-1, which is involved in the production of active IL-1. IL-1 promotes accumulation of more neutrophils and macrophages within the joint. Ingested urate crystals may also rupture phagolysosomes, releasing additional proteases and inflammatory mediators. A vicious cycle develops as newly recruited

inflammatory cells release cytokines, free radicals, proteases, and arachidonic acid metabolites to recruit even more leukocytes. Complement activation by the alternative pathway may further contribute to

leukocyte recruitment. The result is an acute arthritis that typically remits in days to weeks. However, repeated attacks of acute arthritis lead eventually to the formation of tophi, aggregates of urate crystals and inflammatory tissue in the inflamed synovial membrane and periarticular tissue, as well as severe cartilage damage that compromises joint function.
Only about 10% of individuals with hyperuricemia develop gout.
Other factors linked to disease include:
•  Age of the individual and duration of the hyperuricemia. Gout usually appears after 20 to 30 years of hyperuricemia
•  Genetic predisposition. In addition to X-linked HGPRT abnormalities, polymorphisms in genes involved with urate or ion transport and inflammation are associated with gout
•  Alcohol consumption
•  Obesity
•  Drugs (e.g., thiazides) that reduce urate excretion

Four clinical stages are recognized:

after menopause in females.

localized hyperemia and warmth, and, occasionally, mild fever.

resolution of acute arthritis. Some individuals never have another
attack but most experience a second acute episode within months

• Simple karyotype (,20% of sarcomas): Like many leukemias and
lymphomas, some sarcomas are euploid tumors with a single or limited number of recurrent chromosomal aberrations (Table 26.7) that
occur early in tumorigenesis and are specific enough to serve as diagnostic markers. Tumors with these features most commonly arise
in younger individuals and show limited degrees of pleomorphism.
Examples include Ewing sarcoma (described earlier) and synovial
sarcoma. In some cases, the oncogenic effect of chromosomal rearrangements is reasonably well understood (see Table 26.7). In others,
the pathogenic mechanisms are unknown. These recurrent events
often produce a fusion gene encoding oncogenic chimeric proteins,
which represent potential targets for therapy.
• Complex karyotype (,80% of sarcomas): These tumors are usually
aneuploid or polyploid and demonstrate multiple chromosomal
gains and losses, a feature that suggests underlying genomic instability. Examples include leiomyosarcoma and undifferentiated soft
tissue sarcoma. Such tumors are more common in adults and tend
to be pleomorphic.
Classification of soft tissue tumors continues to evolve as new molecular genetic abnormalities are identified. Clinically, soft tissue tumors
range from benign, self-limited lesions that require minimal treatment,
to intermediate grade locally aggressive tumors with limited metastatic
risk, to highly aggressive malignancies with high metastatic risk that are
frequently fatal. All highly aggressive malignancies are classified as
sarcomas, but this term is used less consistently among locally aggressive
nonmetastasizing tumors. Pathologic classification integrates morphologic (e.g., muscle differentiation), immunohistochemical, and molecular features (Table 26.8). In addition to accurate diagnosis, tumor grade
(degree of differentiation) and stage (extent of local and metastatic disease) are important prognostic indicators. The next section will consider
representative soft tissue tumors (summarized in Table 26.8).

TABLE 26.7 Chromosomal Abnormalities in Soft Tissue Tumors
• Simple karyotype (,20% of sarcomas): Like many leukemias and
lymphomas, some sarcomas are euploid tumors with a single or lim-
ited number of recurrent chromosomal aberrations (Table 26.7) that
occur early in tumorigenesis and are specific enough to serve as di-
agnostic markers. Tumors with these features most commonly arise
in younger individuals and show limited degrees of pleomorphism.
Examples include Ewing sarcoma (described earlier) and synovial
sarcoma. In some cases, the oncogenic effect of chromosomal rear-
rangements is reasonably well understood (see Table 26.7). In others,
the pathogenic mechanisms are unknown. These recurrent events
often produce a fusion gene encoding oncogenic chimeric proteins,
which represent potential targets for therapy.
• Complex karyotype (,80% of sarcomas): These tumors are usually
aneuploid or polyploid and demonstrate multiple chromosomal
gains and losses, a feature that suggests underlying genomic insta-
bility. Examples include leiomyosarcoma and undifferentiated soft
tissue sarcoma. Such tumors are more common in adults and tend
to be pleomorphic.
Classification of soft tissue tumors continues to evolve as new mo-
lecular genetic abnormalities are identified. Clinically, soft tissue tumors
range from benign, self-limited lesions that require minimal treatment,
to intermediate grade locally aggressive tumors with limited metastatic
risk, to highly aggressive malignancies with high metastatic risk that are
frequently fatal. All highly aggressive malignancies are classified as
sarcomas, but this term is used less consistently among locally aggressive
nonmetastasizing tumors. Pathologic classification integrates morpho-
logic (e.g., muscle differentiation), immunohistochemical, and molecu-
lar features (Table 26.8). In addition to accurate diagnosis, tumor grade
(degree of differentiation) and stage (extent of local and metastatic dis-
ease) are important prognostic indicators. The next section will consider
representative soft tissue tumors (summarized in Table 26.8).

sarcomas. Pleomorphic liposarcoma is aggressive and frequently
metastasizes.

Leiomyosarcoma
Leiomyosarcoma is a malignant tumor of smooth muscle. It most
often develops in the deep soft tissues of the extremities and the retroperitoneum
of older adults and is more frequent in females than males.
Leiomyosarcomas have underlying defects in genomic stability leading
to complex karyotypes.
MORPHOLOGY
Deep soft issue leiomyosarcomas are firm, rubbery, or fleshy tumors. Histologically,
they consist of eosinophilic spindle cells with blunt-ended, hyperchromatic
nuclei arranged in interweaving fascicles. Brisk mitotic activity and necrosis are
common. Immunohistochemical detection of smooth muscle proteins such as
smooth muscle actin, desmin, and caldesmon can aid in diagnosis.
Clinical Features
A A A

Leiomyoma
Leiomyoma, a benign smooth muscle tumor, most often arises in
the uterus but can occur in any soft tissue site. Uterine leiomyoma
(fibroid, Chapter 22) may cause a variety of symptoms including in-
fertility and menorrhagia. Leiomyoma may also arise from cutaneous
erector pili muscles (pilar leiomyoma) or from deep soft tissues, large
vessels, or the gastrointestinal tract. Germline loss-of-function muta-
tions  in  the  fumarate  hydratase  gene  (FH)  lead  to  an  autosomal
dominant syndrome of multiple cutaneous leiomyomas, uterine leio-
myomas, and renal cell carcinoma. Fumarase hydratase is a Krebs
cycle enzyme, another intriguing example of the link between meta-
bolic abnormalities and neoplasia.
Soft tissue leiomyomas are usually 1 to 2 cm in size and are composed
of fascicles of densely eosinophilic spindle cells that intersect at right an-
gles. Tumor cells have blunt-ended, elongated nuclei with minimal atypia
and few mitotic figures. Solitary lesions are easily cured by excision.

Leiomyosarcoma
Leiomyosarcoma is a malignant tumor of smooth muscle. It most
often develops in the deep soft tissues of the extremities and the retro-
peritoneum of older adults and is more frequent in females than males.
Leiomyosarcomas have underlying defects in genomic stability leading

Deep soft issue leiomyosarcomas are firm, rubbery, or fleshy tumors. Histologi-
cally, they consist of eosinophilic spindle cells with blunt-ended, hyperchromatic
nuclei arranged in interweaving fascicles. Brisk mitotic activity and necrosis are
common. Immunohistochemical detection of smooth muscle proteins such as
smooth muscle actin, desmin, and caldesmon can aid in diagnosis.

Synovial Sarcoma
Synovial sarcoma was so named because in the first described cases,
the tumor involved soft tissues near the knee joint leading to specula-
tion that it arose from synovium. However, synovial sarcoma shows
variable epithelial differentiation and can present in locations that lack
synovium. Synovial sarcomas account for approximately 10% of all
soft tissue sarcomas and typically occur in adolescents and young
adults. Individuals often present with a deep soft tissue mass that has
been present for several years. Most synovial sarcomas demonstrate a
unique chromosomal translocation t(X;18)(p11;q11) composed of the
SS18 gene fused to one of three SSX genes. The fusions encode chime-
ric proteins that interfere with normal chromatin remodeling and
dysregulate gene expression.
MORPHOLOGY
Synovial sarcomas can be monophasic or biphasic. Monophasic synovial
sarcoma consists of uniform spindle cells with scant cytoplasm and dense
chromatin arranged in short, tightly packed fascicles. The biphasic type dem-
onstrates a second component of glandlike structures composed of cuboidal
to columnar epithelioid cells (Fig. 26.46). Immunohistochemistry is helpful in
the diagnosis of these tumors because tumor cells, especially in the biphasic
type, are positive for epithelial antigens (e.g., keratins), thereby differentiat-
ing them from many other sarcomas.
Clinical Features
Synovial sarcomas are treated with limb-sparing surgery and chemo-
therapy. The 5-year disease-specific survival varies from 62% to 83% and
is related to tumor stage and patient age. Common sites of metastases are

Clinical Features
Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcomas are aggressive malignancies
that are treated with surgery, adjuvant chemotherapy, and/or radiation.
The prognosis is generally poor. Metastases occur in 17% to 50% of
cases.
KEY CONCEPTS
Soft Tissue Tumors
• Soft tissue sarcomas are malignant mesenchymal lesions that are distinct
from tumors of epithelial, central nervous system, hematopoietic, or lymphoid
tissues.
• Soft tissue tumors likely arise from pluripotent mesenchymal stem cells
rather than mature cells.
• Tumors that recapitulate a mature mesenchymal tissue (e.g., smooth muscle)
can be subdivided into benign and malignant forms.
• Some tumors are composed of cells for which there is no normal counterpart
(e.g., synovial sarcoma and undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma).

utility.
• Most adult sarcomas are genetically heterogeneous with complex karyotypes,
histologically pleomorphic, and associated with a poor prognosis.

Undifferentiated Soft Tissue Sarcoma
Undifferentiated soft tissue sarcoma includes malignant mesenchymal
tumors that cannot be classified into another category by morphology,
immunophenotype, or genetics. The major subtype, undifferentiated
pleomorphic sarcoma, arises in the deep soft tissues of the extremities,
especially the thigh of middle-aged or older adults. It is an anaplastic
tumor that typically has a complex karyotype due to genomic instability.
MORPHOLOGY
Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcomas are usually gray-white fleshy masses
that may be quite large (10 to 20 cm in size). Necrosis and hemorrhage are
common. Microscopically, they are most commonly composed of sheets of
large, anaplastic polygonal cells with hyperchromatic, irregular, sometimes
bizarre nuclei (Fig. 26.47). Other undifferentiated soft tissue sarcomas may
contain predominantly spindled or round cells. Mitotic figures, including atypical nonsymmetric forms, are abundant. By definition tumor cells lack both differentiation along recognized lineages or diagnostic genetic abnormalities.
Clinical Features
Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcomas are aggressive malignancies
that are treated with surgery, adjuvant chemotherapy, and/or radiation.
The prognosis is generally poor. Metastases occur in 17% to 50% of
cases.
KEY CONCEPTS
Soft Tissue Tumors
• Soft tissue sarcomas are malignant mesenchymal lesions that are distinct
from tumors of epithelial, central nervous system, hematopoietic, or lymphoid
tissues.
• Soft tissue tumors likely arise from pluripotent mesenchymal stem cells
rather than mature cells.
• Tumors that recapitulate a mature mesenchymal tissue (e.g., smooth muscle) can be subdivided into benign and malignant forms.
• Some tumors are composed of cells for which there is no normal counterpart (e.g., synovial sarcoma and undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma).
• Sarcomas with simple karyotypes demonstrate reproducible chromosomal
and molecular abnormalities that contribute to pathogenesis and have diagnostic utility.
• Most adult sarcomas are genetically heterogeneous with complex karyotypes, histologically pleomorphic, and associated with a poor prognosis.

Undifferentiated Soft Tissue Sarcoma

Undifferentiated soft tissue sarcoma includes malignant mesenchymal tumors that cannot be classified into another category by morphology, immunophenotype, or genetics. The major subtype, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, arises in the deep soft tissues of the extremities, especially the thigh of middle-aged or older adults. It is an anaplastic tumor that typically has a complex karyotype due to genomic instability. MORPHOLOGY Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcomas are usually gray-white fleshy masses that may be quite large (10 to 20 cm in size). Necrosis and hemorrhage are common. Microscopically, they are most commonly composed of sheets of large, anaplastic polygonal cells with hyperchromatic, irregular, sometimes bizarre nuclei (Fig. 26.47). Other undifferentiated soft tissue sarcomas may contain predominantly spindled or round cells. Mitotic figures, including atypical nonsymmetric forms, are abundant. By definition tumor cells lack both differentiation along recognized lineages or diagnostic genetic abnormalities. Clinical Features Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcomas are aggressive malignancies that are treated with surgery, adjuvant chemotherapy, and/or radiation. The prognosis is generally poor. Metastases occur in 17% to 50% of cases.

KEY CONCEPTS

Soft Tissue Tumors

• Soft tissue sarcomas are malignant mesenchymal lesions that are distinct from tumors of epithelial, central nervous system, hematopoietic, or lymphoid tissues.

• Soft tissue tumors likely arise from pluripotent mesenchymal stem cells rather than mature cells.

• Tumors that recapitulate a mature mesenchymal tissue (e.g., smooth muscle) can be subdivided into benign and malignant forms.

• Some tumors are composed of cells for which there is no normal counterpart (e.g., synovial sarcoma and undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma).

• Sarcomas with simple karyotypes demonstrate reproducible chromosomal and molecular abnormalities that contribute to pathogenesis and have diagnostic utility.

• Most adult sarcomas are genetically heterogeneous with complex karyotypes, histologically pleomorphic, and associated with a poor prognosis. SELECTED READINGS Antonescu CR, Dal Cin P.
